In this study, we investigate and mitigate systematic biases in the vector magnetic field measurements of the sun. These biases, which affect all vector magnetographs, stem from the vector inversion process and the use of specific polarization detectors. By examining the effect of these biases on data obtained from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we demonstrate that the B field in the line-of-sight component of a typical 180-degree sector is consistently overestimated by approximately 10-15 Gauss. Conversely, in the U and V components, a bias of approximately 5 Gauss is observed. Furthermore, we show that the Spherical Harmonic Coefficient Transformation method effectively reduces these biases in the B field, with a margin of error of approximately 2 Gauss, and approximately 1 Gauss for the U and V components.

A novel technique utilizing game theory has been developed to independently manage
a large two-way energy demand side without compromising user comfort. By integrating
a predictive model of energy consumption into this framework, consumers can make
informed choices about their energy usage in response to the energy price. By viewing
energy usage as a non-cooperative game, each user seeks to minimize their energy cost
while competing with others to draw the most energy at the lowest price. An iterative
algorithm employing the best response equilibrium concept has been devised to solve
this problem, allowing users to optimize their energy usage. To account for user comfort,
a comfort factor has been incorporated into the model, and a priority order has been
established for real-time energy pricing to accommodate varying levels of comfort.
Simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in reducing overall
energy costs and distributing savings equitably among users.

The unification of quantum mechanics and general relativity is a critical issue in modern physics, with the analysis of black holes in various theoretical frameworks offering valuable insights into the relationship between the two. The unification of these theories is particularly challenging, with the analysis of charged black holes in the Rastall theory of gravity presenting a promising avenue for understanding their impact on the black hole equation and Hawking radiation. The analysis of these black holes in the context of the universe has far-reaching implications, with the analysis of their behavior and properties providing a window into the fundamental nature of spacetime. The analysis of these black holes is a critical component of the search for a quantum theory of gravity, with the analysis of their behavior and properties providing a critical component of the search for a quantum theory of gravity.

We delve into the convergence speed of the ergodic average in finite von Neumann algebras, and establish a algebraic framework to analyze spectral transformations in the ergodic theorem. We also demonstrate that non-commutative tools can be applied to the study of time series, and provide a new method for analyzing the autocorrelation function's convergence rate in the univariate Gaussian case.

The Gaia BP/RP spectra cover a broad wavelength range of 285-345 nm, which is an ideal area of the spectrum to detect metal-poor stars. By analyzing the characteristics of these stars, we can identify metal-poor stars within the halo and the globular clusters of the Milky Way. To do this, we created a machine learning model that uses a specific set of features derived from the spectra, which can distinguish metal-poor stars from hotter or cooler stars. By applying this technique to a sample of 1,000 stars, we found it to be 94% accurate in identifying metal-poor stars. Furthermore, we applied this technique to the Gaia DR3 catalog, which contains the positions and distances of 1,000,000 halo stars. By combining the metallicity data with the positions of these stars, we found evidence of a substructure within the halo of the Milky Way, which is characterized by a shift in the distribution of the stars.

The frequency and severity of extreme fire events are increasing globally, a trend linked to the effects of climate change. This phenomenon is observed across diverse regions, which are highly susceptible to wildfires due to their ecological and economic significance. A novel large-scale analysis of fire activity has been developed, combining land surface conditions and weather forecast data to evaluate daily fire risk across the globe. This approach, based on MODIS satellite fire counts, enables the monitoring of fire activity, the identification of high-risk periods, and the adaptation to changing environmental conditions. An analysis of fire data from 2012 to 2022 reveals a substantial rise in fire activity in Australia and North America, with Australia experiencing the most extreme fires in its recorded history. This trend is projected to continue, with significant variations expected in the coming years.

Language complexity is a key aspect that has been studied extensively, yet there's no universally accepted definition. This research identifies and categorizes the various factors of complexity, particularly those of morphological complexity. It examines and compares different metrics that aim to quantify specific factors, such as the diversity and variety of word forms within a language. By correlating and validating these measures, the study seeks to clarify what each one actually measures and how they relate to particular aspects of language complexity.

Galaxy cluster mergers resulting from gravitational collisions can be influenced by self-interacting dark matter with self-interaction cross sections ranging from 0.1 to 10 square centimeters per gram, unlike cold dark matter which lacks self-interaction properties. We examine galaxy cluster mergers in small scales to investigate self-interacting dark matter, which may be detected through X-ray observations of shock fronts and infrared observations of the colliding galaxies. Utilizing high-resolution simulations, we analyzed four galaxy interactions and identified two pairs that exhibit self-interacting dark matter signatures. Furthermore, observational analysis of 18 galaxy interactions in six clusters in the Milky Way's vicinity revealed four interactions consistent with self-interacting dark matter, whereas eight remain consistent with cold dark matter, and six are too uncertain to draw conclusions.

We develop and examine a novel approach to compress POMDPs by leveraging the structural characteristics of POMDPs with limited observation capabilities. Building on recent breakthroughs in POMDP compression for models with discrete states and continuous rewards, we extend these results to POMDPs with restricted information and introduce a new model compression algorithm that maintains a constant level of approximation error. Theoretical analysis confirms the validity of our method and illustrates the effects of various parameters on the compression performance, which in turn guides the selection of optimal parameters. Our method is also applied to several benchmark problems from the Spine Library to evaluate its efficiency, and provide a comparison with the best available solutions.

M-estimation provides a robust approach to statistical analysis, capable of withstanding outliers and non-normal data. However, existing research on robust M-estimation for independent component analysis is limited. Furthermore, most previous studies assumed that source signals followed specific parametric distributions, a restrictive condition often not met in practical applications. To address these gaps, this research proposes a new method for analyzing mixed data with a non-normal robust M-estimation approach, particularly suited for non-symmetric data distributions. The proposed rapid ICA method leverages an optimal-weighting least absolute deviation estimator to achieve better performance compared to traditional techniques, as demonstrated through several numerical experiments. The results show rapid convergence and improved accuracy with the suggested method.

Traffic incidents are a leading cause of congestion on urban roads, causing delays and increased costs. To mitigate these effects, it is crucial to provide timely updates on traffic conditions to drivers. Real-time data collection through geotagged social platforms can help achieve this, but identifying traffic incidents across different areas and timeframes poses a significant challenge. In response, we have developed an algorithm that leverages social platform data to pinpoint traffic incidents instantly. Our proposed method utilizes a multi-instance linear regression model to identify incidents based on traffic sentiment and movement speed. We tested this approach on two cities, comparing its performance against existing techniques and found that it significantly increased the accuracy of identifying traffic incidents.

The paper focuses on a specific type of elliptic partial differential equation that involves a measure defined on the boundary of a given domain, similar to the Dirichlet-Neumann problem, but with a more generalized approach. Unlike traditional problems, we do not assume the boundary has any specific regularity properties. The study proves the solution's regularity up to the boundary under certain conditions on the involved coefficients and also investigates the stability of the solution with respect to these coefficients.

Firstly, we employed genetic algorithms to identify promising cobalt-rich materials within the ytrium-cobalt-boron system's chemical space. The emergent coverings of Y-Co-B exhibited enhanced stability and exceeded the cobalt saturation observed in ytrium-cobalt-boron compounds. Upon further investigation via density functional theory, several of these high-cobalt density materials were found to have the potential for storing 500 Wh/kg at standard conditions, surpassing the current limitations of ytrium-cobalt-boron alloys. The discovery of these new cobalt-rich materials was facilitated by the innovative exploration of the Y-Co-B system's chemical space, which also uncovered additional stable materials, including cobalt and a new ternary compound. The presented work showcases the potential for rapid materials discovery through the analysis of chemical space, which can uncover novel functional materials and uncover hidden compositional relationships within complex alloy systems.

Real-world bidding situations often involve uncertain factors such as uncertain budget and uncertain clicks. The absence of a universally applicable solution to account for these factors has led many practical applications to develop their own methods. In this paper, we establish a comprehensive mathematical model to determine the optimal bidding strategy that minimizes the risk of exceeding the budget while achieving the best return. Our risk-aware optimization problem is broken down into a series of return-based sub-optimization problems. By transforming this problem into a quadratic programming problem, we can derive an efficient and closed-form solution. Our experimental results demonstrate that our approach is effective in addressing the challenges of budget management in real-world bidding situations.

To achieve precise control over quantum systems, a long-standing theory suggests employing a strategy involving negative Wigner functions. Although numerous examples demonstrate the feasibility of guiding quantum particles with such functions, there have been few comprehensive examples on a theoretical level. We've developed an example of guiding a quantum system featuring significant Wigner negativity, showing that significant precision can be achieved without employing operators that increase energy. Moreover, through both linear and non-linear approximations, negative Wigner features are found to enhance the maximum attainable precision by a factor of two compared to positive functions. Furthermore, we've identified that the most effective potential profile for achieving high precision is nearly identical to the lowest eigenstate of the system's Hamiltonian when it's in a state of high negativity.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) systems utilizing privacy enhancement techniques on non-uniform random sources may inadvertently generate internal side effects that jeopardize security. The problem arises when trying to assess a QKD system's security with approximate models that neglect these side effects. In a study, researchers developed a general analytical framework for evaluating the privacy enhancement output of quantum sources with various distributions, including log-normal, uniform, and arbitrary distribution. The researchers also investigated the impact of different parameters on security and system performance and highlighted potential risks associated with using non-uniform sources. The study's findings are applicable to both self-phase modulation and electrical bias modulation sources.

This study reveals that a Lorentzian 3-manifold contains a Bertrand curve family if and only if the curve is a planar spiral. We further establish, within any Lorentzian 3-manifold, the presence of a specific family of plane screens, and we determine the necessary conditions for a Lorentzian surface to contain a Bertrand curve.

This paper's main goal is to investigate the combination and sampling distributions of Feller diffusions, focusing on the distribution of particle counts over time. Feller diffusions, being self-interacting stochastic processes, have been utilized to model various phenomena such as population growth, population collapse and biological inheritance patterns. The study begins by examining Feller diffusion characteristics, including initial conditions, conservation laws, and key properties such as non-explosion, critical mass, and macroscopic mean field equations. The paper then explores the combination distribution of identical Feller diffusions, as well as the distribution of a single particle given a specific number of particles, utilizing generating functions. The results are applied to notable examples, including Yule processes, population processes with competition, and stochastic models of population growth/decline. The analysis is further supported by numerical simulations conducted using Python.

We introduce an innovative method for analyzing the scattering of a single excitation within a generic quantum system connected to a guided wave. Our approach involves an intuitive diagrammatic technique that enables us to derive a comprehensive set of equations for determining the reflection and transmission coefficients at different points along the waveguide. We apply this method to investigate the limits of linear and non-linear scattering processes, providing insights into high-order scattering phenomena. Additionally, we conduct numerical simulations to validate the applicability of our findings to non-trivial scattering of multiphoton Fock states through a Y-junction quantum system, utilizing a triple quantum dot setup to modulate coupling.

In the context of Dirac's dual role for particles and antiparticles, we've established a theoretical framework for Bohr-Kroning diffusion of dark energy with boosted spin characteristics. Our findings reveal that, in the case of neutral particles, the energy density is directly related to the Laplacian of the Newtonian potential, while for charged particles, the relationship involves the Laplacian of the Ricci curvature. As dark energy density increases, it results in an acceleration of the universe. Our calculations show that for bosons, the parameter $\alpha$ is equal to $-1$, whereas for fermions, $\alpha$ is equal to $-2$. Additionally, we've established a relationship between the curvature parameter and the dark energy density parameter.
We start by introducing Faulhaber's sum of powers formula, then discuss how Fermat, Newton, Bernoulli, and Euler contributed to its development and understanding.

This study explores the performance of differential modulation techniques for Continuous Phase Modulation (CPM) without encryption and presents an enhanced differential detection method that outperforms conventional non-coherent approaches in terms of bit error rate at specific signal-to-noise ratios, while achieving similar results with only a minor loss in signal power.

A key challenge in reinforcement learning is obtaining a reward function that users find acceptable.  Traditional methods for getting this reward involve asking for scalar preferences, but this can be time-consuming and may not accurately represent the reward.  To address this, a new approach uses composite preferences, which consist of multiple scalar preferences.  To make learning with these preferences more efficient, we developed an innovative method that involves clustering trajectories based on their features and then asking for visual preferences over the resulting clusters.  This allows users to provide more meaningful feedback and reduces the overall learning time.  To incorporate these visual preferences, we developed a novel reward function that combines several rewards, each associated with a different preference order.  To train the reward function, we used a multi-objective reinforcement learning from human feedback algorithm that learns to satisfy the scalar preferences based on the visual preferences provided.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted experiments on simulated environments and found that it significantly reduces training time and leads to better alignment with the desired feedback.

This study examines the impact of noncommutative space-time on the nucleon's structural functions, specifically its wave function and mass decomposition. To achieve this, we employ vector and axial currents in conjunction with the commutative space-time as a reference point. Our analysis reveals that noncommutative effects manifest as expansions in terms of the noncommutative parameter $\theta$, influencing the nucleon's configuration functions. To determine these effects, we utilize QCD sum rules to compute the relevant correlation functions.

Using a modified toric code on a 3D honeycomb lattice deformed into a torus, we investigated a novel topological phase called the topological edge phase. The phase exhibits two distinct ground states and hosts edge excitations on flat and curved surfaces. Our results show that the topological edge phase can be achieved solely through local star operators on an open, flat surface, provided that specific, non-planar graph structures are employed. Furthermore, the persistence of this topological phase under significant lattice distortion demonstrates the robustness of its properties.

We establish bounds on the free energy and resolvent of a specially designed class of random block matrices, whose components have limited scope. These matrix components consist of large sparse matrices with added complexities of a relatively small number. Our proof employs previously developed techniques, along with a crucial concept of self-consistent independent matrices. These self-consistent matrix concepts facilitate the creation of a controlled comparison between the original matrix ensemble with its simplified, self-consistent counterpart. As a result, we establish the concentration of the free energy within mesoscopic scales, which in turn enables us to derive large deviation estimates for the spectrum. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that the spectral statistics of these random band matrices are accurately approximated by those of a standard elliptic sigma-model originally proposed by Fyodorov. These findings are further supported by numerical experiments.

The recent surge in success in the field of conversational language processing is largely attributed to the advancements in pre-trained language models. However, the evaluation of these models in conversational settings remains a challenge due to the lack of comprehensive benchmarks. To address this issue, we propose a new pre-training task, known as Meaningful Word Substitution (MWS), which offers a more significant semantic understanding by focusing on the meaningful relationships between words. Our proposed MWS task is demonstrated to be a better learning objective compared to the widely used Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task, particularly in the context of conversational pre-training. Furthermore, we introduce a new benchmark, the ParlerEval, which builds upon the Wiki Conversations dataset and provides a diverse set of questions to assess models' abilities in conversational understanding. Empirical results show that our MWS pre-training objective outperforms the widely used BERT and the recently proposed BERT-like conversational pre-training models, achieving substantial improvements of 20.2% and 8.3%, respectively, according to the F1 score metric.

The increasing use of data-driven decision-making has led to a surge in interest in interpretability. However, the current approach lacks a standardized method to measure interpretability, making it difficult to compare different algorithms. To address this, we've developed a framework that evaluates the complexity of human learning for tree-based models. By combining elements from information theory and learning theory, our framework allows us to calculate the 'cognitive intricacy score,' a metric that measures the effort required for a human to learn and understand a given algorithm. We've used this framework to compare four tree-based models, revealing that simpler algorithms are more easily interpretable.

An unsupervised algorithm called Isolation Forest (IForest) is used to detect anomalies in complex datasets. IForest works by recursively splitting data instances, with anomaly scores assigned based on path lengths. I've created a new, lightweight version called TiWS-iForest that operates efficiently in resource-constrained environments. This algorithm combines IForest with a lightweight classifier to improve detection in weakly guided situations, where limited labels are available. I've optimized IForest's anomaly scoring, considering memory limitations, and incorporated an adaptive guide to reduce the need for extensive training data. This enhanced algorithm was tested using real-world datasets, with results showing its superior performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods.

A novel Bayesian time-dependent extreme value model is presented, which treats observations in a specific time frame as instances of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. The model's parameters are estimated using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods through the Bayesian approach. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method effectively recovers true parameter values even with infrequent extreme events. Additionally, the proposed method is applied to analyze daily precipitation data in London, UK, between 1869 and 1900, revealing significant model improvements.

The concepts of "optimal" or high cross-section areas are defined based on a constraint of accessible phase space, and these definitions are applied to analyze the cross-section of reactions involving area-selective phase space constraints. It is demonstrated mathematically that areas with stationary average cross-section values correspond to the geometrically defined shapes and confirm certain commonly accepted notions.

This study presents COMET-ATOMIC, a vast and meticulously annotated common sense knowledge base. Our work discusses the development of COMET-ATOMIC and its capabilities, including the capacity to efficiently handle user queries. Furthermore, we introduce COMET-ATOMIC's two cutting-edge NLP tasks: zero-shot and first-shot question answering. Our network, consisting of 254 million entities and 3 billion relationships, surpasses ATOMIC in terms of common sense reasoning performance. Our research showcases the distinct advantages of incorporating COMET-ATOMIC into machine learning models, particularly in visual question answering, where it yields significant accuracy boosts.

The Hi-GAL survey has gathered the most comprehensive data to date on Galactic
hotcore sources, using data from the Herschel space mission. The survey's full
dataset is now publicly accessible, encompassing all the data processing steps
from initial image reduction to final source extraction. This technical paper
outlines the reduction process for the Hi-GAL survey, including details on the
data cleaning procedure, source extraction, and the creation of the reduction
pipeline that will facilitate future large-scale surveys.

The globular cluster NGC 2808, observed by the VISTA Variable Star Survey, contains an unusual spread in horizontal branch stars. This variation in metal content is unusual for a globular cluster, and researchers have been studying it to understand the underlying causes. A study has now provided new data on the metal content of stars from the cluster's original population, using the VISTA data, and found that the metal content of certain stars is consistent with previous measurements. This supports the conclusion that NGC 2808, despite being a globular cluster, has a metal content range that is unusually wide.

A well-known phenomenon, Single File Diffusion, is characterized by the inability of particles to pass one another, and its consequences are extensively studied. Researchers have developed various models to analyze the distribution of the time particles spend moving after an initial release. Our study, however, examines the time particles spend moving after initially exiting a confined space. Using both computational simulations and analytical models, we investigate how this "Initial Exit Duration" phenomenon behaves in different models. Our results reveal that a specific entropy-related factor significantly influences this duration. Additionally, we have created mathematical tools to calculate and study the distribution of the time particles spend moving after both initial release and exit. Our findings are consistent with experimental data and can be applied to understand the movement of particles in complex environments.

Quantum mechanics' non-commutative nature means the order of measurements impacts results, yet it's unknown if this impact adheres to a unified probabilistic framework, given that different experiments seem to yield conflicting probabilities for simultaneous events. By applying a quantum equivalent of Bayes' Theorem, which incorporates the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics, the contradictions in inference probabilities are resolved, ensuring consistency across various measurement scenarios, and the resulting formula aligns with a Bayesian framework.

This paper examines how the energy density of a system changes under different conditions, focusing on the relationship between energy, temperature, baryon density, and the various properties of the system. By using a model that takes into account quantum effects, we calculate the energy density and compare it to an ideal gas model. Our analysis reveals that when a system is large, the two models produce similar results, but for smaller systems, there are noticeable differences. Specifically, the quantum model shows a difference in energy density that is proportional to the size of the system. This effect becomes more pronounced at lower densities and higher temperatures. We also investigate how the quantum model behaves at finite densities and temperatures, and how it is affected by the quark masses. By studying the relationship between energy density, temperature, and volume, we gain insight into the properties of the system and how it changes under different conditions.

In modular cohomology, Stiefel-Whitney operations play a pivotal role. It has been established that Stiefel operations in the mod $p$ cohomology ring of the Steenrod algebra generate the entire non-trivial elements in the mod $p$ cohomology group. Building on this research, we aim to expand our understanding of the mod $p^2$ cohomology group of the Steenrod algebra. Focusing on the specific case of $p=3$, we aim to identify the 3-torsion elements in its cohomology group. By analyzing the mod 3 cohomology, we find that the cohomology group is generated by a specific set of Stiefel operations, with the only element in the cohomology group being $Sq^2\mathcal{P}^1\mathcal{P}^1\mathcal{P}^1\mathcal{P}^1$.

Recent breakthroughs in all-sky UV imaging satellites have significantly expanded our understanding of the ultraviolet spectrum. Our research introduces a novel filter design, the Lyman-alpha Filter (LAF), specifically engineered to capture  a broader area of the blue-ward profile of hydrogen's Lyman-alpha emission. This enables more comprehensive photometric data to be obtained. Our new filter model incorporates LAF and demonstrates its efficiency through detailed analysis of various celestial objects. This includes real data from galaxy observations and simulated data from galaxies and starbursts. Our results indicate that the LAF can significantly enhance the accuracy of determining hydrogen line ratios in galaxies, as well as improve measurements of hydrogen-to-stellar ratios compared to traditional filters that target the continuum. Our research indicates that the LAF can also provide insights into the effectiveness of hydrogen feedback in starbursts.

This research investigates the issue of regulated output tracking in interconnected network systems through filter estimation and a generalized distributed predictive control approach. By leveraging the properties of automorphism groups, an efficient graph filter estimator is designed, enabling network nodes with identical characteristics to achieve tracked outputs through generalized distributed predictive controllers. Furthermore, our proposed method outperforms previously proposed control strategies, and our results demonstrate that the inner loop stability of the system is guaranteed without requiring minimum phase conditions on exosystems, thus expanding the scope of applicable exosystems.

A picture indexing system efficiently categorizes and retrieves vast collections of images by transforming them into a compact, vector-based format. Traditional systems rely on hand-crafted features, but recent advancements in the field of computer vision have led to the exploration of techniques that automatically learn these features from the images themselves. This research introduces the concept of dynamic picture indexing, where the indexing system is periodically retrained to continuously adapt and improve its performance. We developed an efficient and scalable framework that leverages multiple processing units to rapidly reindex large collections of images, and evaluated its performance using several visual features and different tasks. Our findings demonstrate the benefits of reindexing large datasets compared to reindexing smaller subsets, and highlight the importance of utilizing multiple features to achieve accurate picture indexing.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to securely transmitting a message from a sender to a receiver over a noisy communication channel, employing a method that avoids the need for a shared secret code. Our novel technique utilizes the inherent properties of channel noise to generate a shared secret code between the receiver and sender, thereby ensuring security. By modeling noise as the XOR sum of a shared random process and an unpredictable, independent noise component, we develop a method that enables the sender and receiver to generate a shared secret code through communication of carefully crafted signals. Moreover, we prove that the method maintains confidentiality even in the presence of an eavesdropper who has access to the transmitted signals, using the shared random process available to the receiver, but does not have access to the noise component. Our research also showcases a simple example of how the technique can be applied to the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel, achieving a secure transmission capacity that is within a logarithmic distance of the well-known Shannon capacity limit under conditions where the channel's shared random process perfectly matches the noise component.

We present and numerically validate a new theoretical framework, based on the two-fluid model, to analyze uniform motion in superconducting devices with washboard potential. This model examines the current-voltage relationships of both superconducting single-particle and superconducting superfluid tunnel junctions. The two-fluid two-component framework considers the coherent quantum tunneling and superconducting phase dynamics, resulting in two coupled differential equations that are integrated and compared to existing models and experiments. The research also includes uniform transport in Josephson junctions exposed to magnetic fields, with an emphasis on distinguishing between quantum tunneling and coherent phase dynamics contributions to the resulting patterned resistance.

This study introduces AdaLPRO, an innovative estimation technique with the ability to adaptively modify the smoothing width in local projections to accurately capture impulse response estimates. Impulse response estimates produced by a local projections approach are influenced by the selection of the smoothing width, an optimal balance being sought between capturing short-term and long-term dynamics. AdaLPRO's flexible framework enables the smoothing width to be adjusted across different time horizons, ensuring more precise capture of impulse response estimates. The proposed method is evaluated through extensive Monte Carlo simulations, demonstrating its superiority over traditional shrinkage methods in handling varying dynamics at different time horizons. Empirical applications of AdaLPRO to U.S. data reveal improved performance in capturing the short-term and long-term dynamics of macroeconomic variables following shocks.

The Landau gauge charge in the Minkowski spacetime is investigated, focusing on its Poincaré properties. We demonstrate the role of the electromagnetic field's stress tensor in the Landau gauge charge, showing that the gauge-dependent components can be rendered independent of the gauge by considering a current with compact support. We calculate the angular momentum, highlighting both orbital and spin contributions, and find that the gauge-dependent angular momentum can be made finite and gauge-independent by including the momentum's orbital and Poincaré scalar invariants. We also explore the vacuum's role, showing that the momentum density circulates and generates angular momentum opposing the charge, consistent with angular momentum conservation.

Named entity recognition, a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing, is particularly challenging when dealing with fine-grained entities. The majority of existing models are designed for coarse-grained entities and require adaptation for their application to more detailed entities. Moreover, most current models are based on Euclidean space, which is more suitable for tasks involving coarse-grained entities. In contrast, NER with fine-grained entities is best modeled using a space with distinct inner and outer regions, such as hyperbolic space, which has a negative curvature. This space naturally accommodates hierarchical data, making it an ideal framework for modeling hierarchical entity types. In this research, we introduce FGNET-RH, a novel framework for fine-grained named entity recognition in hyperbolic space. Our framework leverages the inherent properties of hyperbolic space to capture the hierarchical structure of entity types and employs a specific loss function to represent entity relationships. Our experimental results on a subset of the CoNLL2003 dataset demonstrate that FGNET-RH outperforms existing models, such as the baseline model FGNER, by 1.1% in terms of F1 score.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a general class of univalent functions and the second Hankel determinant $H_{2,3}(f)$ has limited upper bounds for functions within the class $\mathcal{U}$ and also for class $\mathcal{S}$. Furthermore, these findings include previously discovered inequalities as special instances.

To accommodate growing customer demands, large cloud data centers are adopting a volunteer approach to load distribution, where a shared backlog of volunteer jobs is allocated to resources based on need. This paper introduces Prepartition, a novel load distribution system that manages these data centers efficiently. Through simulation, we demonstrate that Prepartition achieves significant load balancing and high resource utilization, outperforming other conventional scheduling methods, and results in equitable virtual machine allocation for contributors.

In many strategic interactions, especially when multiple agents are involved, predicting what each will do based on their inferred plans becomes increasingly difficult, especially when there are multiple possible outcomes such as equilibrium states. While simple games can be analyzed using strategies like "best response," more complex scenarios require solving complex systems of equations, as demonstrated in research involving Markov games. Our study introduces the concept of "equilibrium anticipation" as a challenge for AI. We also present the Equilibrium Anticipation Network (EAN), a novel deep learning approach designed to forecast the outcomes of strategic interactions, including both non-cooperative and cooperative equilibria. By employing Theorem 1, we establish a link between the solution of a set of non-linear fixed-point equations and the stationary point of the loss landscape of the EAN. Experimental results confirm the superior performance of EAN in anticipating equilibrium states across various complex games.

A novel, statistically-based approach is introduced to impose constraints on a class of non-negative numbers representing potential causal effects, where an upper limit is established in terms of observable data and an assumed maximum potential correlation among variables. The introduced constraints are determined by this assumed maximum correlation and an empirical lower bound on causal influence is established, based on the variables' joint distribution and the specified maximum correlation. The method's utility in addressing the problem of causal inference in complex systems, modeled using directed graphs with many interconnected nodes, is demonstrated. The method's properties are proven to hold in the context of directed acyclic graphs, while an extension of the method is proposed for systems, modeled using cyclic graphs, that are subject to unobservable external influences.

This study investigates the efficacy of predictive systems for monitoring linear time-invariant systems under conditions of covert attacks. It is demonstrated that when system parameters are known, a two-stage approach combining predictive fault detection with a fault estimator can achieve fault detection with zero false alarm rates, even in the presence of covert attacks. Furthermore, the approach remains effective regardless of the unpredictability of process disturbances. Additionally, the approach is shown to maintain its performance even when disturbed by processes, as long as certain conditions are met, and its results are compared to those of traditional monitoring methods that rely on real-time data.

This paper introduces GAE-ISumm, a state-of-the-art graph-based model for abstractive summarization tailored to 13 Indian languages with limited training data and resources. The model leverages the power of graph neural networks to enhance summarization capabilities by capturing non-local dependencies among tokens, thereby improving overall performance. Additionally, GAE-ISumm benefits from being trained on a monolingual corpus, requiring no domain-specific fine-tuning. The results of our experiments demonstrate that GAE-ISumm achieves superior summarization capabilities, consistently ranking as a strong baseline on datasets from the WMT 2020 and WMT 2021 benchmarks. The model's code and datasets are publicly available on GitHub for further research and development.

A star-srimaly ring, or s-ring, is a left artinian ring with specific properties related to its ideal structure. The ring has an additional operation, denoted as ∘, which maps elements to subsets, influencing both left ideals and two-sided ideals. The concept of noether s-rings is introduced, defined as rings where certain chains of ideals are finite. The study explores the properties of noether s-rings, proving that s-rings of noether type satisfy the ascending condition on members of the family ℱ. The ring is further decomposed into a semisimple ring and a nilpotent ring. The work generalizes known results from s-ring theory, particularly those by T. M. Al-Smadi and K. P. Shyama, and provides a comprehensive understanding of s-ring structure when char(R) ≠ 2.

A recent hypothesis has suggested that an undetected dark matter halo, characterized by a distinct density distribution, could be responsible for the observed stellar dynamics in the solar neighborhood. This dynamic distribution would exhibit reduced central mass concentrations and distances, contrasting sharply with conventional mass distributions. Contrarily, our research challenges this hypothesis by examining the dynamics of five stars within 100 parsecs of the sun, for which we have established rigorous lower mass limits and stringent maximum distance constraints, effectively ruling out the possibility of a hidden mass concentration within these constraints. Consequently, our findings are incompatible with the characteristics of a typical dark matter distribution, thereby casting doubt on the hypothesis of a hidden dark matter halo, and prompting us to explore alternative, more conventional explanations.

Deep learning techniques have become ubiquitous in solving complex problems. The variational autoencoder (VAE) is an advanced probabilistic model that enables efficient inference and parameter estimation. It can be seen as a probabilistic autoencoder that learns to represent data in a latent space. By imposing a prior distribution on the latent variables and minimizing the stochastic ELBO objective, VAEs strike a balance between reconstruction and inference. This work introduces a new regularization term to the standard VAE model, enabling the direct estimation of per-channel variance in the weight matrix of the decoder, which is further constrained to have a unit Frobenius norm. Theoretical analysis shows that this new objective outperforms the standard VAE in terms of generalization and numerical results demonstrate its efficacy on both MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets.

The rapid growth of the Internet of Things has led to significant innovation in IoT-based applications, particularly in intelligent home systems. However, smart homes face significant challenges in managing numerous IoT devices, many of which are restricted to a single function. To address this issue, this research proposes a private blockchain-empowered IoT system that enhances existing IoT-based smart home solutions. By incorporating a blockchain-based infrastructure, smart homes can now efficiently monitor and control their IoT devices, allowing users to quickly locate missing gadgets and optimize energy usage. Furthermore, the application of private blockchain technology in smart homes empowers them with essential security and privacy features. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed solution, simulations were conducted, demonstrating a substantial improvement in detecting missing IoT devices, with an improvement rate of up to 100% in various scenarios, when compared to a non-blockchain-based approach.

This research introduces a novel method for assigning grayscale values to pixels in images, called deep learning-driven quantization of logarithmic values (DLQ-L), which is an enhancement of the existing quantization of logarithmic values (QLQ) technique. The proposed DLQ-L method utilizes a neural network to learn the pixel value distribution from network training data, thereby optimizing the quantization process. The advantages of this method include reduced bit-depth for pixel representation, enhanced image clarity, and improved storage efficiency. The DLQ-L method is demonstrated to be versatile and adaptable to various image types, including medical images, natural images, and satellite images. The experimental results show that DLQ-L outperforms existing techniques, including power law encoding and quantization of logarithmic values, in terms of visual clarity, color preservation, and data compression capabilities. The DLQ-L method also exhibits superior performance in terms of data compression capabilities, requiring less storage space and bandwidth.

A graph is considered upgradable to a planar graph if it can be drawn without any crossing edges by positioning its vertices at various vertical levels. The problem of determining if a given graph has this property is generally computationally intensive, with a specific version of the problem being proven to be computationally intractable when the number of vertices in the graph is the variable factor. However, this problem becomes more tractable if the number of vertices in the graph is replaced with another variable factor such as the maximum number of edges that converge on the same point in the graph, or the number of cycles in the resulting layout when the graph is drawn without crossing edges.

Crowdsourcing has become a widely used strategy for gathering data from a large number of people, but a common challenge arises from the inconsistencies found in such data. Researchers have been exploring various methods to address this issue, but few studies have focused on dealing with the uncertainties associated with crowdsourced data. In this research, a new, straightforward approach is presented that leverages an ensemble of machine learning models to analyze noisy crowdsourced datasets. This method allows for the analysis of the data's uncertainty by using an entropy-based approach, resulting in "human softmax" distributions. These distributions can provide a more accurate understanding of crowd workers' decision-making processes and the overall system's reliability.

For semiflows with rapid mixing properties applied to various types of spaces including both finite and infinite dimensions, we demonstrate that the transfer operators exhibit exponential reduction in their operator norms when acting on $L^p$ spaces where $p$ is greater than 1.

A covering array with minor strength-2 is a 2-dimensional array where every subarray, created by minor operations on column indices, has all possible values from a finite set covered. There are $|\mathcal{M}_k(n) |$ such arrays for a given value-quantity $k$ and array dimension $n$ over the finite set, where $\mathcal{M}_k(n) $ is the minimum number of rows required. A general recurrence relation and lower bound for minor strength-2 covering arrays are proposed, and specific upper and lower bounds are derived for the minimum array dimension for various value-quantity $k$.

The One-Qubit Model of Quantum Contests is a theoretical framework that uses a two-state coin-contestant system to demonstrate the benefits of being in a quantum state over a classical state. By incorporating nonlocality and entanglement into the model, it has been shown that small changes to the game structure can lead to significant differences in achievable payoffs, specifically when using a specific form of entanglement and a highly entangled state. Our research expands on this by introducing errors into preparation processes and demonstrating that certain combinations of these properties can still result in optimal payoffs, specifically a specific fractional value. Furthermore, our findings also show that analyzing such scenarios is feasible and can be accomplished in a specific type of computational complexity.

In this study, we attempted to recreate the experiment conducted by
Albrecht et al. (2019) which focused on the development of a universal approach
for systematically replicating software crashes through automation. Utilizing the
R programming language, our results showed that our solution successfully
recreated $75.00\%$ of the test cases from the original study, similar to their
outcome of $75.60\%$, while the method of mapping input values proved to be the
most successful strategy for test case replication, accurately replicating
$83.33\%$ of the test cases, or a total of $14$ out of $16$ crashes.

Theoretical models suggest a square-lattice superposer of $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave superconductivity should produce a square-square vortex grid transition. To test this, we performed a series of high-precision magnetization measurements on the high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductor, $\textrm{La}_{2-x}\textrm{Sr}_x\textrm{Cu}_4\textrm{O}_{8-y}$, across a range of strontium concentrations. Our experimental results show that the expected second-order transition from a square to a triangular vortex grid only occurs within a narrow strontium concentration interval, approximately $0.19 \leq x \leq 0.20$. Beyond this interval, the square lattice superposer appears to be disrupted by the presence of additional superconducting order.

Researchers have discovered that thermal photons exhibit a unique flow characteristic that is influenced by the properties of quark-gluon plasma. Through simulations using hydrodynamics, they found that these photons' directionality is highly sensitive to the viscosity of QCD fluids. This directionality can serve as an essential tool to measure the interaction strength between QCD fluids and provide accurate information about their transport coefficients.

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional structure formed from the overlap of three identical triangular lattices, and due to its inherent properties, it's a promising platform for studying exotic magnetic phenomena and their associated quantum phases. A recent study, employing numerical methods, identified a wide variety of stable magnetic configurations in kagome and triangular lattices with short-range interactions. These results were further generalized to encompass longer-range interactions and were found to be both extensive and diverse, with some configurations exhibiting periodic patterns and others exhibiting aperiodic behavior. Notably, one structure exhibited characteristics of a proposed "breathing kagome" arrangement but with differences in the relative magnetization of its sub-lattices.

In large-scale intervention studies, researchers often face the challenge of evaluating numerous interventions without prior knowledge of their significance. To address this, statisticians and data scientists use the False Discovery Rate (FDR) to control the proportion of false positives. However, the conventional FDR methods typically assume independent interventions, which is rarely the case in reality. To bridge this gap, a new approach called Regulated FDR (RFD) was developed to handle dependent interventions. However, the RFD method requires an additional constraint, which limits its applicability. To address this, we propose a novel method called C-FDR, which relaxes the constraint and ensures an FDR less than or equal to the rFDR under dependence. The C-FDR method leverages the interventions' marginal effects to relax the constraint and outperforms RFD in both theoretical and practical settings.

This paper utilizes a nonextensive entropy to model an expanding and contracting universe, where the kinetic energy of particles, measured in eV, is a superior parameter compared to the traditional temperature for non-equilibrium systems.  We expound on this cosmological thermodynamic model, initially introduced in our earlier research paper [arXiv:2007.02439].

The CDF II collaboration's $W$ boson mass measurement deviates from the Standard Model prediction by 7 sigma. A new two Higgs doublet model with non-zero hypercharge is examined in detail, specifically in a context that could resolve both anomalies of the $W$ boson mass discrepancy and the muon $g-2$ anomaly simultaneously. We establish the parameter space that satisfies electroweak precision tests and 2HDM electroweak precision test constraints for a given $W$ boson mass. We demonstrate the capability of the model to reconcile the $W$ boson mass and muon $g-2$ anomalies, specifically in an approximate decoupling limit where the heavy Higgs mass is approximately 1000 GeV. We also explore the implications of the $\tau$ anomalous magnetic moment within this framework, considering the constraints imposed by $\tau$ lepton decays.

Data analysis is frequently hindered by a lack of suitable data or concepts when conducting ad-hoc, individual analyses. This problem is particularly pronounced in complex, multi-dimensional business data environments, where formulating and answering relevant questions is a daily challenge for business professionals. Current search and query refinement tools are often ineffective, while existing query reparsing methods are tailored to specific contexts, such as natural language processing, and require specialized knowledge to implement. This study presents SWIFTER, a novel, search engine optimized for general business data and designed to provide accurate and diverse query suggestions that align with the thoughts of unnamed data analysts, leveraging crowd-sourced insights to enhance its performance.

Effective communication relies heavily on speakers synchronizing their utterances appropriately. Research has identified various factors influencing this coordination, such as turn-taking, but our focus here is on exploring how to measure speakers' synchronization distances. A novel, unsupervised deep neural approach is proposed to learn a universal synchronization distance metric from conversational speech without requiring transcription labels. This metric is evaluated using a combination of automatically-generated and manually-labeled datasets. Results indicate that using neural acoustic features and speaker embeddings enhances the model's ability to learn the distance function, as demonstrated by its successful validation on a combination of automatically-generated datasets. Moreover, our model's performance is comparable to, and sometimes surpasses, that of a baseline model relying on traditional, hand-crafted, and speaker-identity-based features.

A recent public release of the RCSED version 2 toolkit, along with its associated data, aims to enhance transparency in the statistical and uncertainty analysis of electromagnetic black hole images. The steganographic encoding of image data in published black hole images has led to accurate public reconstructions, yet the recent public attempt to analyze recent M87* and Sgr A* observations failed. To promote openness and reliability in research, the repository contains precise analytical tools and the original data required to replicate these results. The resources available in the repository enable the full statistical recovery of both the August 2020 M87* and Sgr A* imaging observations, leading to publications in The Astrophysical Journal Letters and The Astrophysical Journal.

We introduce SSCAP, a novel, unsupervised approach to temporal action segmentation through self-supervised learning, leveraging human action principles of semantic parts and transitions. This method, devoid of manual annotations, relies on the body's visual features extracted from video data. By employing self-supervised learning, SSCAP identifies action components based on their relationships and similarities. We evaluate SSCAP on video datasets from Kinetics-600 and TheCK, demonstrating its superior performance over state-of-the-art supervised methods.

Using the present algebra, we have identified two types of pentaquark states, which are hidden-charm three-body and concealed-charm two-body states. The first type, which is hidden-charm, consists of a di-meson and a single meson, and their behavior is linked to the characteristics of the meson's internal structure. On the other hand, the second type, which is concealed-charm, is made up of a baryon, a lepton, and an antineutrino, which can be related to the quark model of the baryon. We have explored the creation and decay of these pentaquark states, which can be produced through the strong interaction and decay through the weak interaction. These three-body states can be produced through the strong interaction and decay through the weak interaction, resulting in the emission of a lepton and an antineutrino. These pentaquark states, which are hidden-charm or concealed-charm, have the potential to be studied in high-energy particle collisions and may provide new insights into the complex nature of quark interactions.

In computer science education, InBLoCR groups are a widely used teaching method. They facilitate learning through in-class, collaborative problem-solving in small groups. This pedagogical approach is particularly suited for testing education, offering a practical evaluation of students' testing knowledge. Despite its benefits, the inquiry-based learning method's effectiveness compared to other evaluation techniques has yet to be thoroughly investigated. This study aims to address this gap by comparing InBLoCR group testing with other traditional evaluation methods. We conducted an empirical study involving 120 students, who were taught the same testing material using different educational methods. They then completed various testing-related tasks, including an InBLoCR group activity, written exams, and coding tests. Using a multi-criteria decision analysis approach, we analyzed the results and demonstrated that each educational method has its own strengths and limitations. This study provides valuable insights into the effectiveness of different educational techniques and their impact on learning testing concepts.

Domain adaptation is a machine learning concept that involves adapting a model
trained on a source domain with labeled data and a certain data distribution to
a target domain with limited labeled data and a different data distribution.
This can be achieved without retraining the model with access to the source
domain. However, in many practical situations, the target domain does not
provide sufficient target semantic information due to limited labels or data.
To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach called Semi-Supervised
Theory Transfer (S2T). S2T leverages theoretical knowledge derived from the
target domain to enhance the representation of both source and target domains,
utilizing the unsupervised target data available in the wild. By combining
the unsupervised target data and limited source domain knowledge, S2T aims to
generate a theoretical representation that closely matches the target data
distribution. To achieve the transfer of source domain knowledge to the target
domain, S2T employs a target-aware module to adapt the source domain
representation to the target domain distribution. To further improve the
effectiveness of theory transfer, S2T employs a target semantic module to
disentangle and reconstruct target semantic information from the theoretical
representation, using the target semantic information to reconstruct the target
data distribution. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that S2T
achieves significant performance gains over existing unsupervised domain
adaptation methods.

A novel space propulsion system, utilizing gas core reactors as its energy source, is proposed as an alternative to the current nuclear thermal propulsion systems. This advanced propulsion platform offers significant advantages, including enhanced safety, increased power output, and prolonged operational lifespan. Our investigation focuses on developing this advanced system for various applications, such as remote mining, long-term space missions, and interplanetary colonization. We also provide a comprehensive overview of theoretical and practical aspects of this advanced propulsion system, including its design, construction, operation, and maintenance.

Identifying the precise points of interaction within massive astrophysical detectors is a significant challenge, particularly when localizing multiple interactions in neutrino-observation facilities. Our research introduces an innovative neural network architecture, dubbed the domain-informed neural architecture (DINA), incorporating a spherical projection to accurately pinpoint the relevant volume within these vast detectors. By examining two distinct interaction types in liquid argon, we demonstrate that DINA outperforms conventional methods in determining the three-dimensional interaction volumes, particularly when tasked with identifying multiple interactions stemming from the same incoming neutrino.

The study of substellar exoplanets and brown dwarves is limited by the lack of comprehensive data on their atmospheric properties. To address this gap, we present a new database called EXOplInE, which provides accurate absorption spectra for key molecules found in the atmospheres of these celestial bodies. The database covers a wide wavelength range from 0.3 to 25 micrometers and includes data on H2O, CH4, NH3, CO, CO2, and other important molecules. The absorption cross-sections used in the calculation are based on laboratory measurements and are optimized for specific temperature and pressure conditions. The resulting spectra can be used in various applications, including the analysis of transit events, emission spectra, and transmission spectra. The database is freely available online and can be accessed using various formats, including a standard format and various file types such as ASCII and molecular line lists.

Independent of the logic programming community, research has been undertaken 
by researchers incorporating neural networks into AI systems. These studies 
involve anchoring neural networks' predictions to real-world data, 
enabling interpretability and actionable insights. Our investigation delves 
into the integration of propositional answer set programming (ASP) as a 
means to ground neural networks' outputs. Through a unified framework, we 
examine various ASP-based grounding techniques and relate them to 
interpretability objectives within deep ASP frameworks. Additionally, we 
consider the application of ASP in bridging the gap between symbolic and 
subsymbolic AI approaches.

In the field of quantum information theory, a recent breakthrough has been made with the development of universal quantum resource theories, which are based on the idea that all quantum states can be viewed as resources under specific tasks. Despite significant progress, the problem of characterizing the fundamental laws governing these theories has remained unresolved. To address this issue, we investigate the relationship between state transformations and the properties of symmetry groups, which play a crucial role in quantum operations. By examining the infinitesimal level, we derive a mathematical tool called a 1-cocycle that captures the essential features of state conversions. Building on this insight, we establish the first universal law of quantum information, which reveals that a particular norm derived from a certain Lie algebra dictates when one pure quantum state can be converted into another with high accuracy. Our findings have significant implications for quantum information theory, as they provide a new framework for understanding state conversions and reveal connections to existing theories, such as the quantum version of the Schmidt's shifting theorem and a generalization of the majorization principle.

We develop a fundamental framework for model evaluation, utilizing structural models to generate hypothetical data and identifying statistical functionals that capture the essence of a model's predictions.  Our framework enables us to investigate how predictions from a structural model compare to a hypothetical 'true' model based on observed data.  Key insights include the demonstration that a model can be validated without knowing the data-generating process, and the notion that a 'good enough' model can be selected based on specified criteria.  Our framework also facilitates the examination of a model's predictions in light of actual model-specific outputs.  To address uncertainty, we establish the need for assumptions in the absence of 'true' data and provide nonparametric confidence intervals for a class of functionals, including those in machine learning.  Our framework is applied to two examples, including theoretical models in economics and artificial models in machine learning, to showcase its versatility.

We analyze multi-dimensional time series with large observations, incorporating both stable and non-stable components.  In stable series, extreme values are managed by an attractive mean, whereas non-stable series exhibit a distinct mean behavior characterized by a mean reverting process.  Inference in non-stable series is significantly more complex, as they may not have a finite mean, making estimation and inference tasks particularly challenging.  Our research focuses on developing and evaluating the performance of estimators and inferential tools for non-stable time series.  To facilitate this, we establish the asymptotic distribution of key statistical tools, including the sample mean, median, and LAD estimator, and provide a strategy for nonparametric inference applicable to a range of estimators.  To our knowledge, this is a pioneering study of its kind.

We have developed new quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes that support efficient decoding within a linear time frame. Building upon recent breakthroughs in irregular quantum LDPC code research, we developed two innovative decoding methods that ensure all check nodes can be verified in linear time. The first method, named 1-round check nodes, involves limiting the check connections to roughly $\sqrt{\delta_{d}}$ random variable nodes, which allows all check nodes to be verified within a linear time frame. We found that the error rate performance of these code is superior to that of its nearest predecessor, 2-round check nodes, which involved two rounds of check connections. The second method, named variable node trimming, utilizes original regular quantum LDPC codes and incorporates check connections that remove variables with probabilities exceeding 0.5 after the initial flooding decoding step, which still maintains the property of linear time decoding. We observed that the error rate performance of these code is comparable to that of 1-round check nodes. Furthermore, the proposed codes enable the creation of quantum memory with a constant rate and linear code length while maintaining a constant code distance.

This paper examines the problem of finding a distance-$r$ dominating set in graphs, specifically when the distance $r$ is greater than 1. To address this, a problem known as Distributed Distance-$r$ Dominating Set ($\text{DDrDS}_r$) has been proposed, in which multiple agents on a given graph $G$ collaborate to identify a subset of vertices $S$ that guarantee every other vertex is within a distance of $r+1$ from a vertex in $S$. Each agent has access to limited information, specifically about its own identifier and its $r$-local subgraph.

To solve this problem, a distributed algorithm is proposed for high-girth sparse graphs, specifically $r$-regular graphs with girth $r+1$ or higher. The algorithm enables each agent to construct an $O(r \log n)$-local dominating set in $O(r \log^2 n)$ rounds using a shared randomized greedy algorithm. To achieve this, a key step involves constructing an $r$-local dominating set of size $O(r \log n)$, which is achieved by first creating a local spanning tree, then assigning each edge a random value, and finally having the agents select a root vertex and build a dominating subtree.
