We assess the performance of pre-trained language models on few-shot and unsupervised text classification tasks, focusing on the potential of simple fine-tuning techniques and prompt-based approaches. Our results highlight the effectiveness of these methods, with the few-shot logistic regression prompt surpassing the effectiveness of simple fine-tuning in the unsupervised transfer setting. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of a prompt-based approach, using a linear classifier, in the few-shot and unsupervised transfer settings. To facilitate future research, we have created a comprehensive resource, including benchmark datasets and pre-trained prompts for popular language models, which will enable seamless replication and comparison of our findings.

This project showcases a straightforward, adaptable, and efficient system for 
automatically translating spoken German into text, based on open-source 
technologies. We achieved accurate results with a basic but effective model,
utilizing basic word and subword embeddings, as well as a simple attention model.
The integration of word and subword techniques enhances the model's performance 
on shorter word sequences while maintaining its readability. Our open-source 
implementation of the attention-based many-to-many sequence-to-sequence model 
demonstrates competitive performance on the Amazon Mechanical Turk dataset and a 
frequently used development dataset. Additionally, this project provides valuable 
insights and a benchmark for comparing different speech recognition systems.

Our analysis of optical photometry and spectroscopy data for 30 Doradus Be stars, along with HST data, revealed the following findings. By comparing BeX-RF and BeX-Ray luminosity, we observed that the lower luminosity counterparts, specifically those with $L_{\rm X} < 10^{34}~{\rm erg~s^{-1}}$, have the highest X-ray flux and Be X-RF emission, suggesting an origin from circumstellar material. In contrast, the stars with $L_{\rm X} > 10^{34}~{\rm erg~s^{-1}}$ are predicted to have disk-like structures based on their X-ray spectrum, pointing towards the formation of their circumstellar material from a binary companion. Furthermore, we found that the X-ray emission of the studied sample is significantly lower than that of O stars, with the $L_{\rm X}/L_{\rm bol}$ ratio being on average $10^{-7}$, which is in line with the findings of other studies on Be stars and O stars in the same region.

Inverse Text Standardization (ITS) involves converting informal text into a standardized format. In contrast to its textual counterpart, data-driven ITS models encounter a distinct challenge: the lack of aligned informal-formal text pairs. To overcome this limitation, our approach leverages a diverse collection of relevant data not specifically annotated for ITS to improve model performance. We develop an ITS model that efficiently handles various ITS tasks by adapting to different domains of rich ITS data. Furthermore, our innovative data augmentation technique expands the richness and variety of patterns in the input, improving ITS model accuracy. Our experiments on actual and synthetic ITS datasets confirm the effectiveness of our method in overcoming the challenge of limited data.

This study examines the Faber-Krahn inequality for the sequence of first Neumann eigenvalues of the Hermite operator $H_\beta = -\Delta_\mathbb{R}^k + |\mathbf{x}|^2$ within the $n$-dimensional unit hypercube under the Robin boundary condition. Our objective involves comparing the spectral properties of the $n$-dimensional hypercube's sequence with those of the $n$-dimensional unit ball, specifically in relation to the first eigenvalue $\lambda_1(B_n)$ of $H_\beta$ and its comparison with the Faber-Krahn inequality. The research utilizes the symmetrization technique of Riesz to establish the main result, revealing a distinct spectral behavior for the Robin eigenvalues in the $n$-dimensional hypercube in comparison to the ball's eigenvalue $\lambda_1(B_n)$. The behavior of the eigenvalues in the $n$-dimensional hypercube is shown to converge towards $\lambda_1(B_n)$ as $\beta$ approaches infinity, with the eigenvalues being strictly larger than $\lambda_1(B_n)$ for $\beta > 0$ and converging to it in the limit $\beta \to 0^+$. The research also investigates the convergence rate of the eigenvalues in the hypercube towards the ball's eigenvalue $\lambda_1(B_n)$.

The success of Kernels in various fields is largely attributed to their implicit parameterization, which enables efficient optimization. However, the rigidity of symmetric kernels restricts their broader applicability. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new class of kernels termed non-exchangeable tangent kernels (NETKs). These kernels parameterize functions through tangent maps on domains, offering enhanced flexibility. We demonstrate that kernel-based methods utilizing these maps retain well-established theoretical guarantees. To validate the NETK concept, we apply it to existing techniques such as regression and functional data analysis. Furthermore, we utilize non-convex optimization methods to efficiently estimate kernel parameters. Through theoretical analyses and experimental evaluations, we show the advantages of using non-exchangeable tangent kernels.

The concept of non-Hermitian topology, specifically point-gap topology, has received significant attention in recent years. Research has mainly focused on systems described by non-Hermitian Hamiltonians with particle-number conservation, resulting in matrices that exhibit exceptional rings under certain conditions. These rings connect to topological invariants, such as the winding number, which characterize the system. However, when interactions are incorporated into these systems, the exceptional ring collapses, rendering the point-gap phenomenon inaccessible. To address this limitation, we propose a method for achieving topological properties in interacting systems, even when the exceptional ring has been removed, by extending the point-gap concept to include correlated systems. We demonstrate this by examining a one-dimensional lattice model, where the point-gap characteristics can be controlled through the correlated motion of particles, specifically by manipulating the center-of-mass position, which serves as a topological invariant in correlated systems.

This research explores the importance of social characteristics in synthetic speech, focusing on how these traits impact the quality of the final voice output. To achieve this, a method is proposed to train a TTS model with social traits using a dataset that integrates social information. By using a discriminator model, the trained TTS model can generate speech with specific social traits, which can then be combined with a transformer-based model to create diverse social traits from a single TTS model. Experimentation demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in producing socially tailored voice synthesis.

A theoretical framework combining $A_4$ and $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetries is proposed to generate neutrino mass and dark matter through the interaction of these particles. Specifically, our model features a trilinear coupling between the $A_4$ sector and a $U(1)_{B-L}$ Higgs field, which breaks electroweak symmetry and initiates the generation of neutrino mass. Additionally, the model introduces a unique mechanism for generating down-type neutrino masses at the one-loop level and a portal interaction between the dark matter candidate and the Standard Model via a Higgs-like scalar field. Furthermore, the model allows for the calculation of the dark matter relic density, which can be explained by a combination of annihilation processes and decays into light neutrinos. Specifically, our model predicts a dark matter particle with a mass of 100 MeV that can be detected by upcoming experiments such as the PLATO telescope and upcoming direct detection experiments.

Building on the concept of deformation in nuclei, we introduce a quantum mechanical model based on the harmonic oscillator with three degrees of freedom and apply the uncertainty principle for collective variables. Our model incorporates a fundamental length derived from the minimum uncertainty, which significantly alters the energy levels and wave functions of nuclei along with individual nucleon energies. As the nucleus reaches a state of dynamic equilibrium, we obtain the characteristic energy patterns observed in even-even nuclei displaying an $I$ vs. $E$ relationship, and the derived deformation parameters align with those obtained from experimental data.

This paper presents novel methods for creating larger sets of polyphase Golay complementary sets through the use of a specific matrix transformation. Specifically, we demonstrate that applying a Hadamard product with a matrix of ones results in a set of CPGCS, effectively duplicating the properties of the original set. Furthermore, we outline a method for creating multiple CPGCS sets from a single polyphase Golay complementary set with n elements by performing Hadamard products with n matrices of ones.

This paper introduces a cutting-edge method of deep convolutional autoencoders using a
combination strategy to integrate multiple hyperspectral images without the need for
supervision. The proposed approach, referred to as Feature Combination Deep Convolutional
Autoencoder (FCDCAE), involves the incorporation of multiple HSIs through the convolutional
layer, allowing for the efficient reduction of image dimensions. The resulting low-dimensional
representation is then encoded for reconstruction, with the alteration information between
the HSI pairs being extracted from the error maps derived from the encoded and original images.
The alterations detected in each change map are merged using an average pooling technique,
which significantly reduces false alarms. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated
by the analysis of AVIRIS images of the Pima County and Pushing Target areas. The results
show that combining HSI pairs through the deep network enhances detection accuracy and
minimizes false alarms, particularly when compared to the traditional HSI difference map
approach. The analysis further confirms that varying the number of nodes in the hidden layer
affects detection quality, with the 256-node configuration yielding the best outcome.

A thorough examination of the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity in liquids is conducted using an extensive range of simulations, encompassing both truncated potentials for molecular and atomic interactions, as well as various realistic models. These simulations, comprising nearly 1000 cases, reveal a strong, universal correlation between viscosity and residual entropy across all scenarios, particularly visible when visualized through a specific plot. Additionally, it is observed that residual entropy's individual contributions from configuration and momentum are both essential to understanding the relationship with viscosity. Furthermore, the origins of anomalies in viscosity are thoroughly investigated, revealing a significant connection to the repulsive part of the potential. A comparison with alternative relationships is also presented, highlighting the superior performance of the relationship being studied compared to others in the literature.

The standard $\Lambda CDM$ model of cosmology is modified by introducing a mechanism that causes the universe to cycle between periods of cyclical expansion and contraction. During each expansion phase, the universe grows exponentially, but matter and radiation quickly fill the space until the universe shrinks rapidly. This cycle repeats, with each expansion mimicking the characteristics of our current universe. The repeated cycles of expansion and contraction are found to match observations made by the Planck satellite, while also making new predictions for the cosmic microwave background. The model is further found to be consistent with the Hubble constant measurements from the James Webb Space Telescope. The cyclical nature of the universe's expansion history is examined in the context of B-mode polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization polarization.

The Invariant-set hypothesis, proposed by Connes and Richmond, posits that quantum phenomena occur on a curved surface embedded in a higher-dimensional space of classical physics. Previous analyses of this hypothesis have relied on a global perspective of the space. In this work, we delve into the local characteristics of the hypothesis by examining the geometry of the curved surface in relation to the surrounding space's local tangent planes. Our analysis reveals that, in certain regions of the space, the curved surface exhibits extreme warping, and this behavior is intimately linked to the entanglement phenomenon.

Incorporating Neural Networks for Keyphrase Detection on IoT Devices

Incorporating Neural Networks for communication optimization in IoT networks via Keyphrase Encoding (KPE) presents a viable solution. KPE, a form of compression, involves training a Neural Network (NN) on an IoT device to send compressed data only when necessary. However, deploying large NNs on IoT devices poses significant computational challenges. This paper proposes novel architectures for Neural Networks tailored to KPE, specifically designed to operate on resource-constrained IoT devices. These architectures, featuring reduced complexity, require minimal external storage and support both recurrent and convolutional operations. The proposed networks were tested on public datasets, with results showing improved accuracy and efficiency in KPE applications. The experimental results demonstrate that the new architectures can achieve high accuracy while significantly reducing computational requirements.

This research explores the connection between Fermi-liquid theory for 2D fermions and stochastic processes involving dimer configurations on two-dimensional lattices with a background gauge field. It begins with a comparison of the low-energy properties of Fermi-liquid theory with those of the free massless Dirac field, highlighting the statistical mechanics under a gauge field. The discussion then shifts to the isomorphism between Fermi-liquid and Dirac field energies, which is demonstrated using the dimer model on a lattice. The effect of a background gauge field on the critical dimer configuration is also examined.

The Group Lasso method, an extension of the Lasso for grouped variable selection, has several modified algorithms for continuous data. Two recent adaptations for categorical data, the CGL and NGL approaches, utilize imputation with pseudo-values and ignore the nominal nature of data, relying on traditional Lasso for continuous data. Building upon these methods, we propose the IGGL algorithm, incorporating the iterative grouped Lasso, which uses identity imputation of missing group elements for each categorical variable. This approach is further enhanced by providing theoretical justification for its convergence and supporting evidence through simulations and real-world analysis demonstrating its superior performance in variable selection over existing methods.

System reliability is a major concern for embedded real-time systems, particularly those used in safety-critical applications. To address this, a two-phase fault isolation mechanism is introduced, utilizing system virtualization to separate hardware and software faults. Heterogeneous multi-core virtualization enables the creation of isolated regions for real-time applications, allowing the monitoring of hardware performance and fault detection. A central, privileged software layer, running at a lower priority on a virtual core, manages application software as a hypervisor for fault isolation and system reliability. Each isolated software application is assigned a unique security context, enabling the detection of unauthorized access and fault triggering. Furthermore, the system virtualizes memory management, real-time task scheduling, and power/voltage management, and optimizes virtualization overhead through the sharing of hardware and software resources, as well as direct hardware access for fault isolation and scheduling purposes.

Panoramic stitching from multiple images is a fundamental computer vision task. Traditional methods rely on detecting and matching distinctive features, but this can be problematic when features are missing or non-descript. To address this, we've developed an innovative approach that incorporates the principle of gravity to determine camera orientation when only two or more barrell-shaped images are available. By identifying the floor in each image, we can accurately segment the scene and compute camera poses, enabling the stitching of images even in the absence of distinctive features. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we've created a dataset of multi-view images captured indoors and evaluated various stitching techniques.

We introduce the concept of chimeric states in systems influenced by random external factors using two interconnected groups of identical oscillators, subject to identical stochastic influences. Through linear stability analysis, the existence of these unique states is demonstrated, which exhibit group-level synchronization and desynchronization, accompanied by internal phase oscillations. Notably, external randomness has no impact on the boundary defining desynchronized state, yet we identify two distinct boundaries for synchronized state, one affected by stochastics and the other free from it.

In this research, we focus on developing controllers capable of withstanding unexpected disturbances. A key problem we aim to solve involves finding a controller policy that minimizes the average impact of disturbances on system performance, without prior knowledge of their distribution. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework that leverages probabilistic models to search for optimal policies, demonstrating the existence and convergence of solutions. We also present an efficient algorithm that incorporates a model learning component, enabling it to handle unknown systems. Through simulation and experimentation, our proposed methods demonstrate superior performance, achieving better resilience against disturbances, improved data efficiency, and more generalizable results compared to existing techniques.

A new algebraic structure known as multi-layer diagrams forms a monoid under a specific operation of combination, which is related to the Kauffman polynomial. We establish that this new monoid is isomorphic to a desired structure and use it to define rings associated with classical and linkless knots and links based on a specified set of elements within it. These new rings generalize the Milnor variables of the link homology called Khovanov theory and demonstrate specific properties in relation to the link homology called Khovanov-Rozhkov homology, which in turn recovers the link homotopy group $\pi_0(S^3/S^1)$ when considered over a specific field of characteristic 2.

Bekenstein-Hawking entropy in holographic theories exhibits unique properties in response to spatial deformations. When considering the region outside a black hole, the entropy changes in accordance with the area of the region and its gradient, but this behavior is disrupted at the horizon where it's shielded from incoming change. An analogous phenomenon occurs in unitary systems, where the refracted entropy proposed by Lashkari, Liu, and Veltman captures the change in entropy in conformal field theories under spatial deformation. Within this study, the concept of refracted entropy is applied to quantum systems derived from complex networks of tensors, revealing that the refracted entropy provides a more precise understanding of entanglement within these systems. Notably, the agreement between the refracted entropy and the entanglement entropy in planar and spherical geometries is found to be significantly accurate.

Complex systems consisting of interconnected elements are frequently analyzed using stochastic methods to account for unpredictable fluctuations. Nonetheless, random behavior is typically seen as detrimental to systems that evolve according to stochastic rules. Our research demonstrates that distinct and diverse patterns can arise from stochastic dynamics and highlights the significance of information dynamic within random processes. We introduce the idea of information entropy rate to quantify information flow in stochastic systems and reveal that patterns which can sustain and transmit information are influenced by both the system's design and the nature of the random events. We apply this concept to various biological and ecological models, including a graph diffusion model, a birth-death process, a Markov chain, and a system modeling neuron membrane potential, and show that information-carrying structures within these systems are comparable to structural features that are subject to evolutionary selection through information theory.
We introduce an algorithm to produce and display the inverse images in 3D of the H\'{e}non map with general parameters, and we apply it to examine the H\'{e}non map with its original parameters.

We present a clear, exclusive method for calculating the gravitational holonomy along any given curve. This approach draws on a specific function representing the non-commutative geometry of the underlying connection. Additionally, we explore an alternative approach to understanding the AS-holonomy through an alternative representation of the AS-algebra as a deformation of the functions on the underlying manifold.

We are examining specific factorial distributions in relation to 2- and 3-power forms among various types of hooks, such as single, double, triple, and quadruple forms. These distinct categories have been defined previously by different researchers, with single, double, and quadruple forms discussed by Stanley, Krattenthaler, and one of the authors of this current research. Our research focuses on specific factorial distributions regarding 2- and 3-power forms. A generating function for specific partition counts with factorial constraints is derived. The obtained results provide new infinite product identities. The research also yields combinatorial interpretations of the findings. The obtained generating function enables the determination of asymptotic behavior using saddle point methods. The obtained results provide bounds for specific asymptotic behavior. The research also discusses unique phenomena regarding 3-power factorial distributions, such as a sign change in the generating function coefficients.

The spin Larmor clock method is used to measure tunneling time based on the interval between tunneling particles with opposite spins. A new theoretical framework is proposed to explain deviations from the traditional Landau-B\"{u}ttiker-Schroedinger (LBS) model in non-relativistic tunneling scenarios. By introducing spin Larmor clocks, this framework resolves challenges in analyzing fast-spin particles and is applied to a range of complex Hamiltonians, including the Pauli equation in uniform electric fields and the Schr\"{o}dinger equation with position-dependent mass. A comparative analysis of these models with the Landau-B\"{u}ttiker-Schroedinger model reveals a more reliable and accurate approach to tunneling time measurement.

The internal wavefunction of a quark-antiquark pair, specifically in an L=1 state, is characterized by a rapidly decreasing dominant twist distribution $D_1^{\rm dom}(z)$ with a deviation from 50/50 quark-antiquark momentum sharing $|z-0.5|$. This contrasts with its S-wave counterpart, where $D_1^{\rm dom}(z)$ exhibits a symmetric profile around $z=0.5$. As a result, $D_1^{\rm dom}(z)$ in both $\Psi(4415)$ and $\Y(4148)$ exhibits L/R asymmetry, suggesting a significant presence of second-dominant twist distributions. This characteristic may be indicative of the L/R asymmetry of second-dominant twist distributions in other $L=1$ states, such as $\U(4019)$, $\V(4143)$, and \B$(4337)$, of which only the $D_1^{\rm dom}(z)$ profiles exhibit L/R symmetry.

The behavior of Bose-Einstein condensates in a double-well system is examined for two scenarios: when one side is vacant and when both sides contain atoms. Our analysis shows that a quantum phase noise source can act as a nonlinear frequency modulator, switching between the two wells. In the case where one side is empty, this switch occurs via a phase-sensitive parametric process, while in the case where both sides contain atoms, it happens through a nonlinear Rabi oscillation, controlled by the noise strength and the interaction parameter.

We begin by reviewing key concepts in soft theorems, demonstrating their connection to conservation laws at null infinity and the asymptotic BMS algebra. Next, we introduce a model action featuring both a massless and a massive scalar field, which is designed to reproduce the leading double soft graviton theorem through its pole structure at momentum space. This model action also adheres to a gauge symmetry with characteristics reminiscent of the BMS algebra.

To address the challenge of learning multiple tasks sequentially in a single network without forgetting previously acquired tasks, an innovative online ensemble approach has been developed. This method allows the network to retain knowledge from all tasks learned so far, while adapting to new tasks in real-time, using a approach that is on par with an ensemble of individual networks, but with significantly reduced computational requirements. A key feature of this method is its ability to assign a specific importance value to each task, enabling the learning of both correlated and unrelated tasks efficiently. This method has been extensively tested and evaluated using a range of benchmark datasets, including letters, bit vectors, emotions, and CALTECH 101 images, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency.

We define and analyze the properties of generalized geometric shapes, associated with four-dimensional Einstein metrics in a compact, boundary-free setting. Initially introduced in [arXiv:2001.01127], this concept is further developed to establish connections with the work of Bär [arXiv:0903.0971]. We demonstrate that these generalized shapes possess non-trivial and non-zero characteristics, including their diameter, Hausdorff distance between distinct shapes, and the diameter of their respective metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, we present and examine a family of Ricci-flat Einstein metrics in eight dimensions, characterized by their non-trivial geometric shapes and spectral properties of cross-permutation matrices.

In this paper, permutation functions and their relative difference sets in $\mathbb F_{q^{3}}$ are examined. We also establish sufficient conditions for the complete permutation functions in the form $x^{k}$ with $\gcd(2, q) = 1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^{3}}$. Furthermore, based on differential uniformity, we identify and categorize the permutation properties of four categories of functions in $\mathbb F_{q^{3}}$. As an additional contribution, we have shown that four distinct relative difference sets with sizes $(q^{2} + q + 1, q + 1, 3)$ can be obtained from the relative difference sets associated with the non-permutation functions.

This research introduces an automated system for classifying intestinal worms in medical endoscopy videos, an area of significance in the field of medicine. The proposed deep learning architecture, known as the deep belief network (DBN), is capable of accurately identifying and categorizing three distinct types of intestinal worms. By training the DBN on a dataset of 1,200 frames, the model achieved a 96.66% classification accuracy, demonstrating its potential in the accurate diagnosis of intestinal worms.

This research introduces a type of non-zero-sum stochastic game featuring both jumping and regime-switching dynamics, comprising a reinsurer and a reinsured party who negotiate and analyze negotiation outcomes through equilibrium strategies and social optimal strategies, and further investigate these strategies under various scenarios including social optimality, fairness, and efficiency. The paper presents a new estimation method for the game's value based on M-estimation, leveraging empirical measure and weak convergence properties, before concluding the section by analyzing the asymptotic normality of the estimator.

This study develops a novel flight control method using adjustable wings, combining genetic algorithm-based flow field prediction and an advanced dual simplex algorithm. The GenSima method integrates the Genetic Algorithm into the finite volume method to streamline the computational process and lower memory requirements. The algorithm dynamically adjusts the computational grid based on the flow field characteristics, eliminating unnecessary calculations in low-flow regions. The approach is validated using a stochastic dual simplex algorithm and applied to the control of a 2D airfoil. The results demonstrate the method's ability to enhance flight stability and adaptability.

The characterization of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy levels is essentially defined by the scalar and vector couplings to the $\sigma$ and $\omega$-nucleon interactions, which also have the dominant contribution from the $\pi-\omega-\nu$ vertex.

The upcoming CMS phase-1 pixel detector is set to revolutionize particle reconstruction, with its cutting-edge sensors incorporating advanced in-situ calibration and real-time monitoring capabilities.  Despite these groundbreaking features, its complex design and diverse integration into the CMS tracker pose significant reconstruction challenges.  A newly proposed algorithm for the CMS phase-1 pixel detector aims to streamline reconstruction by leveraging the CMS phase-1 pilot edge scan matrix, which will be implemented in the CMS clusterization algorithm to correct for misaligned and defective pixels.

Active galactic nuclei in galaxies formed at redshifts less than one are being studied through optical imaging data, and our goal is to determine the impact of these nuclei on the observed shapes of these galaxies during the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey era. By analyzing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Survey, we identified approximately 100 active galactic nuclei over six months and evaluated the effect of these nuclei on the shapes of their host galaxies. Employing a machine learning approach, specifically the Fast Convolutional Neural Network, we classified approximately 1000 galaxies into early and late types. We discovered that active galactic nuclei are more commonly found in early-type galaxies. Furthermore, we discovered that these nuclei in early-type galaxies tend to slightly distort the shapes of their hosts. However, these changes are significantly less pronounced in late-type galaxies. These findings suggest that early-type galaxies are better suited for accurate measurements of active galactic nuclei centers.

At low momentum transfers, atomic substructures give rise to correlations. Focusing on a two-sphere arrangement, its phase-space distribution is studied. Drawings based on various measures of uncertainty illustrate properties such as entropy, entanglement, and area when different configurations of the phase-space distribution are adopted. It becomes apparent that uncertainty entanglement reaches its peak at Heisenberg's limit, while entropy and area reach their minimum at this point. Measures of uncertainty are compared to assess the similarity between atoms in such configurations.

Achieving fair outcomes in deploying Artificial Intelligence systems is a pressing priority. Researchers have recently focused on achieving equality in prediction outcomes regardless of the target group. However, existing definitions of equality are limited to binary classifications. Many real-world AI applications involve more intricate assessment systems, necessitating the consideration of classification into multiple categories or ordered classes. To address this limitation, we propose a novel co-domain equality framework tailored to equalize predictions across any target group, encompassing both categorical and ordered classifications. Building on this foundation, we introduce the concept of complex-valued deep learning as a novel approach to trained models. By utilizing complex numbers, we can develop representations that are inherently invariant to group identity, achieving co-domain equality without extensive pre-processing or post-processing adjustments. Our solution is validated through comprehensive experiments on a range of datasets, encompassing classification and regression tasks, as well as representations that are deliberately designed to induce bias.

The 30 Dor nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud houses a notable cluster of low metallicity stars, encompassing a broad range of chemical elements. By examining unevolved stars within this cluster, we aim to uncover the nuclear processes responsible for elements' abundance variations. Using a diverse set of stellar models, we simulate the evolution of chemical elements during core and H/He burning phases. Our findings reveal that a star's mass, chemical composition, and mixing processes influence the post-processing of chemical abundances. We observe a narrower abundance range in low mass stars, characterized by a narrow spread of iron abundance, whereas neutron capture elements exhibit a broad abundance range. This abundance spread is attributed to a star's final mass and mass loss. Moreover, we discover a narrow, mass-dependent abundance ridge in neutron capture elements, with a substantial contribution from core processing. Our study underscores the necessity of accounting for final mass and initial chemical composition to accurately interpret abundance spreads in low metallicity globular clusters.

This research introduces a comprehensive toolbox, known as ML-Scorecard, for assessing the performance of binary machine learning models in terms of post-actualization even scoring rules. Each component within the scorecard is designed to evaluate the models' behavior in specific segments of the population based on the predicted outcome probabilities. The comprehensive scorecard, consisting of multiple metrics, offers a more balanced and accurate assessment of the models' performance by allowing for a comparative analysis of different models. The proposed scorecard is demonstrated through a practical application in a financial literacy forecasting scenario using a diverse dataset from the United States and Europe.

This research introduces a new, SQUID-based quantum learning algorithm inspired by combinatorial optimization principles. As quantum technology continues to evolve, it is poised to surpass classical computing capabilities, necessitating careful evaluation of potential threats to information security. To address this, we propose a SQUID-based encryption scheme and examine its theoretical limits through comparisons to computational complexity models. Our analysis reveals that the SQUID-based encryption scheme can be compromised by a Gröbner basis attack in classical computing, but is vulnerable to Grover's algorithm and the Hidden Subset Problem, respectively, when exploited by quantum and optical computing systems. Furthermore, leveraging Shor's algorithm, we demonstrate a polynomial-time solution to the Hidden Subset Problem, outperforming existing quantum algorithms like Grover's and Fourier sampling.

Two new submanifold classifications have been identified in a nearly contact manifold: the pointwise semi-slant submanifolds. They involve cases where a submanifold has neither a global slant nor a global slanting angle. We investigated the geometric properties of product submanifolds under a distorted product structure. Specifically, we identified the distilled product distorted productwise semi-slant submanifolds. We then established and tested various constraints on their geometry.

A rising interest in inactive nuclear recoil examination arises from byproducts resulting from various sources, including low energy signals utilized in the study of dark matter, radon isotopes, and other related fields. We introduce a new method utilizing a wide array of in situ spectroscopic techniques to detect and quantify inelastic nuclear recoil scatters within a diverse range of samples, including geologic and environmental materials. Our approach combines the advantages of existing methods, such as acoustic and optical detection methods, with the added benefits of analyzing color centers within solids. By leveraging the versatility of this method, we are able to detect recoil events that were previously undetectable, opening up new avenues of research in multiple scientific areas.

We examine the movement of a particle with a certain level of energy in a less energy-powered type of particle solvent. Our findings indicate that the particle's movement is influenced by the distribution of powered and non-powered sol particles and is influenced by the particle's energy level, leading to directed movement. By using theoretical methods based on particle forces and simulations using molecular dynamics, we have investigated the particle's movement. We have identified how the particle's movement responds to changes in temperature, particle size, and density of powered and non-powered sol particles. The results show that the particle's movement is influenced by the distribution of powered and non-powered sol particles and is not simply a result of thermal movement. The findings also reveal that the particle's movement can be controlled by adjusting the particle's energy level, providing a potential method for controlling particle movement in a range of applications.

The emergence of magnetorotons in fractional quantum Hall states is a crucial aspect of their excitation spectrum, but as we increase the strength of Landau level mixing and move away from the spherical Hartree-Fock ground state, additional magnetorotons may appear, particularly in systems with fractional charges where they exhibit distinct characteristics. This paper explores the excitation spectrum of both even and odd-occupied fractional quantum Hall states, where multiple magnetorotons are present, by extending spectral calculations to account for their influence. This approach is based on a phenomenological model that aligns with microscopic theories and numerical results, allowing us to calculate the spectral patterns in 2D fractional quantum Hall states. This model is particularly useful in understanding the spectral patterns of real-world samples.

Identifying and containing emerging epidemics is a pressing challenge for epidemiologists. Noticing the initial surge in cases and establishing an effective chain of transmission are key steps in controlling outbreaks caused by infectious diseases. Researchers have developed clustering methods to analyze simulated data and real-world time series, leveraging network models where nodes and edges represent individuals and potential interactions. Our research introduces a novel approach for identifying clusters in growing epidemics on evolving contact networks, combining the strengths of greedy clustering methods and growing network patterns. Our algorithm's results on simulated outbreaks match or surpass existing solutions, and when applied to real-world data, it successfully identifies clusters of infectious disease patterns, offering a promising method for tracking and containing outbreaks.

When creating maximum likelihood maps for CMB experiments with scanned fields of view, a technique called 'X-es' is used to identify and mitigate scanning system errors by linking them to field rotation. Although the method is generally effective, it may be less efficient in experiments with limited data, such as those with sparsely sampled sky coverage or multiple connected detectors, causing the error models to be underdetermined. To illustrate this limitation, a study analyzed simulated full sky maps with a point source at the celestial pole using the Planck experiment's scanning pattern and scanning system error amplitudes comparable to the actual mission. The simulations revealed that a standard approach of 'X-es' with separate error amplitudes for each field of view led to significant bias in temperature anisotropy power spectra, particularly affecting higher multipoles. In contrast, using 'X-es' with shared error amplitudes for connected detector pairs mitigated this bias. The simulations further indicated that while bias in temperature anisotropy power spectra could be reduced, a residual bias persisted due to incomplete coverage.

In goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, agents are guided by language descriptions, but natural language's ambiguity complicates the interpretation of these goals. We propose a novel language model trained on human data that aims to minimize goal description ambiguity. The model generates spoken instructions from computer task states, which humans then repeat using different phrasing. We developed an algorithm that incorporates these rephrased instructions as a form of observation, effectively addressing ambiguity. This approach also enhances sample efficiency in goal-conditioned tasks.

We present the state based tomography of quantum channels utilizing the "stochastic shadow" method, where previous stochastic methods are derived from representing channels as states, now referred to as process states. Process states are naturally obtained from measurements performed with the same POVM. We demonstrate that the previously proposed shadow method's efficiency in quantum state tomography is transferable to the previously introduced dynamical classical channel estimation, where the obtained estimator is "quantum" in nature. We also show that the previous stochastic methods fail to provide an unbiased and efficient tomography of quantum channels, as they lack sufficient information. We also show that our method enables efficient estimation of process states representing channels without requiring any specific physical properties or structures. We also show that our method enables efficient estimation of unitary channels.

The specific geometric Keen inequality, first proposed in a particular case, is extended to all planar convex shapes, demonstrating a more comprehensive relationship between the Cheeger constant and other important characteristics, including the first non-zero Dirichlet eigenvalue, mean width, perimeter, and area. Our proof utilizes a newly established lower bound for the Cheeger constant, derived from an innovative method of inscribing a circle and a regular triangle within a plane.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly being considered for applications such as emergency medical services and surveillance services. In the case of applications where service must be delivered to remote locations, it can be advantageous to utilize multiple UAVs, where one flies at a higher altitude to serve as a relay for the others. This paper focuses on developing an optimal pathway for a single relay UAV to follow, ensuring it can provide the best possible service to a predetermined location. The pathway is computed to minimize the amount of time the relay UAV is present above the service radius, while also accounting for constraints such as battery life and UAV movement speed. The effectiveness of the proposed solution is evaluated through simulation.

The critical behavior of interaction-restricted bilayer graphene is investigated using the renormalization group approach. Specifically, the stability of the four-body coupling within the renormalization group flow was examined. The four-body interaction exhibits a Coulomb-like divergence under high-energy renormalization when layer exchange symmetry is taken into account. The renormalization group flow analysis also revealed the instability of the four-body coupling exponent, $\nu$, with four- and five-body interactions driving it toward fractional values. The four-body interaction instability can be attributed to the presence of massless fermions, indicating a potential physical phenomenon.

The double fullerene conformation of Sc2TbN@C80, which was initially thought to be stable, undergoes a significant structural alteration when it is placed on an h-BN/Ni(111) substrate. Using advanced imaging techniques, our research reveals that the double fullerene transforms into a distinct icosahedral 222-isomer, which was previously unknown. Moreover, the transition between these two configurations is observed to be temperature-dependent, with the process being both reversible and highly specific to the substrate. This study provides valuable insights into the complex interplay between the internal structure of the double fullerene and the external environment, which could have significant implications for the development of advanced molecular devices.

This study examines the fundamental principles of lightweight cryptography, its essential features, and the criteria used to assess it. The underlying concepts of AES-ECB, Hill cipher, and AES-PBKDF2 are thoroughly analyzed through mathematical equations and practical examples, including demonstrations of their operation and associated vulnerabilities. These analyses are supplemented by accompanying Jupyter Notebook code and instructional guides for replication.

To determine precise physical constants, Ramsey spectroscopy serves as a highly effective tool. However, the optimal number of phase evolution times to include in a sequence of measurements remains a matter of debate. Building upon the approach introduced by Geraci et al. in 2019, we have developed a novel, flexible, and statistically rigorous method for trial sequencing in Ramsey spectroscopy. This method allows for adaptive optimization of the phase evolution interval based on the measured signal's autocorrelation properties. Through a Bayesian framework, we conduct multiple trials with varying durations, continuously refining the experimental parameters to achieve the most accurate results. The technique's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and actual field-based geophysical tests, where it successfully estimates tidal geophysical signals with enhanced accuracy.

Network centrality metrics assess the importance of nodes within a network, often based on distance. Existing metrics, however, only capture a single, global scale. By incorporating the triangle inequality, we can analyze networks at both global and local scales. A multi-scale centrality measure emerges that combines node distances with the triangle inequality, effectively capturing essential network properties. This metric leverages the variability of inequality across triangle centrality distributions, and demonstrates correlations with various real-world characteristics, including disease transmission and information flow.

A novel metric tensor has been developed with the characteristics of azimuthal symmetry and metricity. This gave rise to a new equation of motion for the metric tensor, which was then simplified under specific conditions. These circumstances involved an ultra-relativistic and static gravitational field, resulting in a particular metric tensor form. This formal is comparable to that found in general relativity but differs in an essential aspect: the presence of additional static fields. A non-zero, constant value for another field has been determined, which is analogous to the role of Newton's gravitational constant in general relativity. This new approach to gravity is therefore analogous to Newton's theory, yet is more comprehensive. An analysis of the Schwarzschild solution has been conducted, which has led to a new interpretation of black holes. A discussion on the azimuthally symmetrical theory of gravity has also been provided.

To extend the concept of equivalence classes for matrix pencils, we propose a notion of rigorous equivalence, which compares entire sets of matrix pencils simultaneously. This concept has implications in completing missing matrix pencils within a set characterized by some entries. A prior study by the authors established the matrix pencil completion problem's solvability and identified structural constraints for completed matrices, now, we demonstrate that the set of matrix pencils satisfying these constraints forms a single class under rigorous equivalence.

We've established a mathematical equivalence in a cohomologically trivial manifold $M$ - a key aspect of twisted tori - to a specific type of twisted geometric structure incorporating a triangle of related components consisting of form, metric, and connection. This triad, formed by pre-geometry concepts, outlines the rules for $M$'s twisted geometry. Our research extends this framework by incorporating two geometric transformations, forming a triangle of geometric equivalences including $M$'s twisted geometry itself. The geometric twistorialized geometry and dual topological geometry, both defined by twisted structures with distinct triangles of twisted data, are identified as key dualities in this framework. The twistorial geometry is fully specified by the twisted geometry's rules but expressed in a distinct geometric language. Conversely, the dual geometry is defined by two twisted triangles, providing twisted rules that can be translated into traditional geometric language. Our research extends this framework by incorporating $M$'s twisted geometry as well, completing the triangle of geometric equivalences.

A few years ago, Demaine et al. proved a significant conjecture by Robertson and Seymour, establishing that any finite graph can be embedded into a specific type of metric with only slightly larger distances. This was done by using a bounded treewidth structure. Conversely, another study found evidence suggesting that even the simplest proposed method for achieving this was likely to fail. However, recent findings have shown that a more sophisticated method is indeed feasible, resulting in a new discovery. Furthermore, a different discovery has shown that not all graphs with non-negative curvature can be embedded into low treewidth metrics with minimal distortion, but interestingly, hyperbolic graphs have this property, which was also proven that even graphs with a limited rank cannot be distorted with polynomial factors.

In discrete-time systems, the smooth, strongly monotonic functions have a distinct dynamical characteristic that differs from their continuous-time counterparts. Unlike in continuous systems, cycles of any form can occur in the discrete setting. This distinct nature has significant implications for the long-term behavior of these systems. Notably, for a system defined on an unbounded region of n-dimensional space, the attractors of almost all orbits exhibit an intricate relationship with hyperplanes, indicating a pervasive and fundamental pattern that permeates the system's dynamics.

The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) is a widely used hybrid algorithm for quantum computers. A common strategy to improve its performance involves the use of parameterized quantum techniques. However, this paper presents an innovative VQE variation that bypasses parameter optimization. Instead, it employs a quantum-based method to directly measure the vibrational eigenstates of molecules within their electronic ground state. The proposed method utilizes the time evolution of the molecule's first excited electronic state to create adaptive generators for eigenstates. An numerical simulation demonstrated the effectiveness of the algorithm, showing that it can produce accurate results for small molecules. Furthermore, the method's requirements for mid-circuit measurement and qubit coherence are evaluated. The results suggest that the algorithm may be a more suitable choice than other VQE variations for certain molecules, especially those with low coherence times.

A widely accepted principle in machine learning suggests that MAP estimates of learned representations should be utilized by decoders for optimal performance. However, under this assumption, the decoder must rely solely on these estimates and has no other means of gathering supplementary information. This paper introduces a novel approach, dubbed The Profound Generative Decoder (TPGD), which allows the decoder to learn from and exploit the underlying structure of the representation, thereby gaining access to additional information. In experiments, we found that multiple TPGD instances consistently outperformed state-of-the-art decoders across various real-world and synthetic datasets, both in terms of training and testing. Notably, our results demonstrate that even a fixed, non-informed MAP estimate can be surpassed by a second-order probabilistic model when paired with the same representation.

The Hubble tension is a significant problem in modern cosmology, stemming from discrepancies between Hubble constant measurements from local and early universe observations. The local measurement using Hubble's original method exceeds early universe measurements based on the Planck mission's cosmic microwave background data by a significant margin. A proposed theory suggests that a stochastic gravitational wave background could potentially resolve this discrepancy by increasing the value of the Hubble constant from early universe measurements by a substantial margin. This gravitational wave background could originate from inflation, and its amplitude depends on the inflationary scale. A model has been proposed to explain why different gravitational wave modes have varying sensitivities, resulting in a rigid-amplified shape. This model assumes that the wave background is a result of a shift in the primordial power spectrum after inflation, caused by a change in the scalar field's effective mass. The zero mode of this change corresponds to a stochastic gravitational wave background, and its shape is flat. A non-zero mode results in a white noise contribution, and the combination of these two modes produces a rigid-amplified shape. This gravitational wave background could be detected using NANOGrav's pulse timing array and the cosmic microwave background, and its existence could be confirmed by the presence of a specific correlation in the data.

Interferometric observations of molecular emissions from the comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) were made using the ALMA Atacama Compact Array on April 1, 2017, at a distance of 0.52 astronomical units. The observations focused on CO, CO+, CS, and H2O molecules, and the resulting data were analyzed to understand the comet's activity and composition. The data were compared with those of other comets, and a correlation was found between the CS production rate and the comet's activity, as well as its distance from the sun. The results suggest that CS is produced in the comet's nucleus, and that its production is driven by the same processes that produce other volatile species, such as CO and H2O. The findings have implications for our understanding of the comet's composition and the distribution of volatile species in its nucleus.

This study presents a straightforward and efficient method for generating speech without the need for closely paired audio and text. Two essential components are introduced: a text-to-sequence model that creates diverse and coherent text sequences from seed words, and a voice conversion module that transforms audio recordings into a standardized form. When given a written sequence, the system can then produce audio by combining these modules. We demonstrate that the developed system can produce engaging audio representations from an extensive collection of speech samples. Furthermore, our developed text and speech sequences surpass random ones in evaluation metrics, indicating their high quality.

This article explores the effectiveness of Tsallis entropy under the assumption that a long-range scalar field has a complex quintessence energy density. By considering the Tsallis generalization of the 2nd law of thermodynamics in Tsallis holographic dark energy models, the research focuses on the behavior of Tsallis entropy when the Tsallis index q approaches 1. A modified Friedmann equation is derived, and its implications for various equation of states are examined using complex quintessence. This leads to a study of the stability of these models in the context of background perturbations in the Tsallis entropy under complex quintessence energy density scenario.

Multi-objective Mixed Integer Non Linear Optimization problems are common in real-world applications such as real-time energy management, power scheduling, and building energy control. To address these complexities, researchers have developed the $\epsilon$-Pareto Front, which involves generating a set of optimized solutions with an error margin. This study proposes a novel approach, the Branch and Bound $\epsilon$-Pareto Front, which integrates multi-objective evolutionary algorithms and guides them towards optimized solutions. The proposed algorithm was evaluated and demonstrated superior performance when compared to the state-of-the-art $\epsilon$-Pareto Front with Particle Swarm Optimization.

We demonstrate that linked Lie groupoids possess a synthetic differentiability structure, which not only ensures individual integrable horizontal paths are globally integrable but also that any application of the source map to an infinitesimal direction implies the integral complete of that direction, making the Lie groupoid integral complete in synthetic differentiability.

The widespread use of wearables, mobile devices, and ubiquitous computing has resulted in an exponential increase in accessible health data. Despite the potential for mobile health applications to improve patient care, the development of seamless data exchange infrastructure has been hindered by the lack of standardized data sharing. This research introduces the concept of Cyber Infrastructure Gateways (CIGs) to create unified access points for diverse data sources, thereby streamlining data exchange and analysis. We demonstrate the applicability of this approach in a real-world scenario involving a mobile health app that monitors glucose levels, showcasing how it can enhance user experience and enable efficient data integration.

In Aspect Sentiment Analysis, classifying aspects' explicit sentiments, such as food quality, according to sentiments, such as good or bad, poses a significant challenge due to the difficulty in identifying implicit sentiments. For instance, a statement about food quality can convey negative sentiments indirectly. To address this challenge, we suggest a new pre-training method called SUPRE, which incorporates supervision to help the model understand implicit sentiments by focusing on the sentiment words within noun phrases. We utilize a novel, large-scale dataset created from online reviews to further support our approach. Through pre-training with SUPRE, we significantly improve the performance of Aspect Sentiment Analysis, as demonstrated by our extensive experiments on various real-world datasets.

To address issues with power and bias in mediation analysis with case-control samples, we investigated how this design impacts identification and computation of key effects, such as total and natural direct/indirect effects. A two-stage approach for examining total effects was identified in previous studies, and we expanded upon this framework to develop three-stage methods for determining all three NDEs in cases where the mediator is binary and noise is present. A critical finding in our research indicates that total sample size is the crucial factor influencing statistical power for NDE estimation in case-control samples, highlighting the potential benefits of efficient sampling strategies. Furthermore, we demonstrated that efficient sampling can reduce variance for NDEs under specific conditions, such as when sampling strata are comparable in size, but may lead to bias in the estimated total effect on an observed scale. To mitigate this issue, we proposed efficient sampling alternatives, such as post-stratification adjustment and weighting, which can yield unbiased and efficient estimates of the total effect while maintaining conditional unbiasedness for NDEs.

This study proposes a robust multiuser transmission strategy for secure communication networks that utilizes reconfigurable intelligent surfaces and suffers from imperfections in nonlinear amplifiers. To achieve this, we develop a joint optimization framework that simultaneously determines optimal beamforming vectors for the access point and the phases of the RIS, aiming to maximize the minimum secrecy rate among all connected users. The complexity of this optimization is mitigated by reformulating it into a second-order cone conic program. To further improve performance, we propose an alternating optimization method that results in conic programs requiring efficient computational solutions. The performance of the presented approach is validated through simulations comparing it to an ideal linear system and a traditional linear amplification-based system. The simulations demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in terms of improved and maintained performance.

To improve the accuracy of feedback for reinforcement learning agents, a straightforward approach involves summarizing and relabeling feedback after the fact. This type of feedback, which is considered noisy, consists of observations about a robot made by people who are not working with the robot. By resampling and relabeling this feedback, a more precise understanding of the environment can be achieved, leading to improved learning outcomes. A key challenge in leveraging this feedback lies in its indirect nature, as it is based on a different experience than the agent's. To address this, a new value function has been developed that focuses on a singular, most likely experience, rather than the traditional feedback-based policy. This new function, named Executive Ability, uses a filtering process to identify and prioritize future feedback that is likely to provide valuable insights. A simulation study has demonstrated that incorporating Executive Ability into a reward-matching algorithm yields significant improvements, with an increase in performance of up to 100% in some cases.

The solar breeze, a fundamental component of the heliosphere, is a critical area of study for heliophysics, but its complex nature poses significant challenges in understanding the solar system's corona and wind. To address these challenges, NASA's Parker Solar Probe mission aims to gain a deeper insight into solar breeze characteristics and the mechanisms driving its formation. To this end, analyzing large-scale properties, such as energy flow, is a promising approach to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the solar breeze. This study employs PSP's electromagnetic field data to calculate energy flow in the inner heliosphere, using a newly developed method that accounts for both in situ and cross-term observations. The results indicate a consistent pattern of energy distribution, with electric field energy decreasing and magnetic and plasma fields increasing as heliocentric distance increases. This suggests a magnetic cascade process, driven by MHD turbulence, rather than a reverse cascade. Furthermore, this study highlights the significance of considering various observational factors, such as varying plasma conditions and spacecraft positions, to gain a more comprehensive understanding of energy flow in the inner heliosphere.

To generalise noncommutative principal bundles, which don't have a clear spatial form, we develop conditions on actions of countable groups on C*-algebras to represent them as cross products. These conditions enable us to establish a one-to-one correspondence between locally trivial bundles and specific types of group actions, preserving properties even when those actions aren't strictly continuous. Moreover, we demonstrate how this theory applies to both continuous and discrete groups, showing the relevance of our results in various contexts, such as actions on commutative C*-algebras and the relationship between cross products and transformation groups.

In the realm of infinite cardinal arithmetic, specifically within the context of P-ideal reality, we establish new relationships between the ultrafilter number u and the nearly disjointness number nd. We-1) demonstrate that u can be expressed as a product of nd and a smaller cardinal less than or equal to chi, the character of ultrafilters; 2) under the assumption of P-ideal reality, we prove that nd is equal to min{u, ap.

The $q$-deformation parameter is employed to examine its effect on Debroglie wavelength in $q$-deformed optomechanical systems. Within a cavity containing a two-level three-dimensional $q$-deformed harmonic oscillator and a harmonic membrane, a optomechanical coupling occurs. By applying the Born-Markov approximation and linearizing the optomechanical oscillators' dynamics, researchers establish fast and slow light conditions within the system. In systems with fast light, absorption, dispersion, and tunneling phenomena are investigated and analyzed. In contrast, in systems with slow light, analogous tunneling and absorption/dispersion effects are investigated. Notably, in both fast and slow light conditions, tunneling and absorption/disapersion occur at the same position. Furthermore, researchers demonstrate the ability to control fast and slow light conditions using control fields and optomechanical frequencies.

Within the Dual-Rotors Model, a comprehensive examination of the 1- and 2 negative parity scissors modes, categorized under R-parity is in progress. Although these modes are inherently undesirable, their development and characteristics are being scrutinized. A thorough analysis of the 1 negative adverse R-parity scissors mode is conducted, with particular attention paid to how it behaves in relation to other modes, such as the gamma Ray Scissors Mode (GSM), its radial partner, and the 1 negative positive R-parity gamma Ray Scissors Mode (GSM*). These modes are identified within the Dual-Rotors Model, along with their corresponding radial partners. Furthermore, the GSM and its radial partner are explored in depth, with their behavior in terms of amplitude and energy being investigated. Energy and amplitude curves for the GSM, its radial partner, the 1 negative adverse R-parity scissors mode, and its radial partner are generated. Additionally, the wave functions of the 1 negative adverse R-parity scissors mode are obtained for selected nuclei.

A novel cell-mean based neural network (CMBNN) is introduced to solve hyperbolic, elliptic and parabolic partial differential equations with various boundary and initial conditions. In contrast to conventional neural networks such as the finite difference method, CMBNN is applicable to arbitrary geometries and can be used in conjunction with an irregular mesh. By employing a cell-averaged approach, CMBNN is able to achieve superior results in complex problems. We examine the theoretical underpinnings of the CMBNN framework, including proof of convergence and stability, and highlight the method's capacity for total variation diminishing. Furthermore, we showcase the method's ability to resolve challenging problems such as the Burgers equation, by comparing it to established schemes such as Kurganov-Tadmor and Harten-Lax-van Leer-ERI.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC is focused on the study of the quark-gluon plasma and will enhance its capabilities in particle detection and data processing beyond LHC Run 3. The upgrades to its detector and luminosity systems, as well as the development of advanced computing techniques using AI and machine learning, are key to improving particle identification and analyzing track and collision data in real-time. The proposed solutions involve integrating advanced hardware and software technologies, and are aimed at addressing a rapidly growing challenge in high-energy physics.

A particle interacting with the Rindler vacuum experiences an entanglement between its past and future light cones due to the timelike Unruh effect. We demonstrate that this effect results in a geometric phase arising from the causal structure, represented by the difference in the lengths of the light cones, which can be quantified by the difference in their areas.

We are excited to present a large and diverse dataset of real-world events, spanning multiple languages and encompassing over 17,000 events in total. This comprehensive event dataset, named MEE, outlines events and highlights essential information such as event participants, location, time, and duration. Our data spans multiple domains and covers the years 2019-2021. We anticipate that this resource will greatly benefit the research and development community, and we look forward to collaborating with you.

We prove that the integrated Chern forms of a generic global vector bundle over a compact manifold are positive eigenforms. This builds on past research that established pointwise positivity for specific characteristic forms. Our findings also show the importance of integrated forms in representing geometric multiplicity, particularly in high-degree hypersurfaces and projective varieties. Additionally, we provide a new interpretation of push-forward forms in characteristic zero, relating integrated Chern forms to Schur polynomials and spectral measures from curvature matrices.

The blazar, Cyg X-3, exhibits a remarkable correlation between its X-ray and gamma-ray fluxes, which reverses with a time delay during certain phases. This phenomenon is attributed to a "stellar breeze" model, in which an time-variable accretion disk wind interacts with the surrounding stellar wind to create a massive reservoir of hot plasma. In this framework, the electromagnetic radiation from the bulk Compton scattering of disk photons by electrons in this wind produces an intrinsic gamma-ray component, while external modulation by the stellar wind produces a modulated component that varies in amplitude depending on the phases. We investigate this phenomenon in an analogous system, in which the black hole in Cyg X-3 is replaced by the stellar black hole, Cyg X-1, which is in a hard state. We demonstrate that the spectral evolution of the disk photons and the modulated phase's intensity and time delay of the spectral evolution provide a self-consistent evidence for the stellar breeze model.

The inclusion of a specific ether-like soul within the Euler-Heisenberg Lagrangian has been explored for its impact on various physical systems, particularly at finite temperatures, and when considering the movement of charged particles within the systems. By introducing this non-abelian term, researchers have discovered significant changes in wave propagation dynamics, and even the possibility of forming bound states between photons and the ether medium at high temperatures, thus potentially leading to the observation of novel physical phenomena in the systems.

A proposed framework for conducting universal syntax and syntax tree analysis was developed and tested, which can be applied to any language provided the language's grammatical rules are known. The complex task of universal syntax analysis has been broken down into two simpler tasks: identifying the correct grammatical structure and then using a collaborative process to determine the correct sequence of phrases. Additionally, a semantic analysis was implemented that leverages the collective knowledge of multiple algorithms to interpret the meaning of sentences in the target language.

The core collapse supernova event, specifically the rapid rotation of the collapsed object, results in the formation of a protoneutron star that transforms into a rapidly spinning and magnetized compact object. This object's rotation leads to the formation of a transient, hot accretion disk that can interact with the surrounding material. We're examining the role of magnetic fields in this process, focusing on the interaction between the accretion disk and the outer boundary of the simulated supernova ejecta. We're investigating two distinct cases: one where a rapidly spinning and weakly magnetized black hole forms, and the other where a rapidly spinning and highly magnetized protoneutron star forms. We're analyzing the effects of these interactions, including the potential for powerful ejections and the impact of these interactions on the simulated supernova event. We're comparing these results to the properties observed in supernova remnants and gamma-ray bursts.

We've identified large early-type galaxies in the HSC-SSP DR6 catalog, focusing on tidal features in their outer regions. By examining tidal features in detailed HSC imaging, we've determined the fraction of these galaxies with such features exceeding 10\%, which amounts to approximately 10-15\% across three redshift intervals: 0.05-0.1, 0.2-0.3, and 0.5-0.6. This indicates that the presence of tidal features decreases significantly with increasing redshift. Furthermore, by examining HSC imaging and stacking data, we've found that the light from these galaxies is predominantly concentrated in their central regions, which suggests that tidal features contribute only a small fraction of the total flux. Additionally, our findings reveal that approximately 60-70\% of large early-type galaxies with tidal features exceeding 10\% are likely the result of a major merger event, rather than just the ongoing process of a tidal merge.

A theoretical model of a static, self-gravitating body in a relativistic framework predicts that the density of such a body decreases as a power of its radius, with a negative exponent, as the radius increases, approaching the boundary. This behavior is a direct consequence of the unique gravitational laws governing this scenario. The model's solution reveals a remarkable phenomenon: as the exponent changes, the classical theory of general relativity breaks down at a certain threshold, resulting in the expulsion of test particles from the body. This threshold corresponds to an exponent larger than 4/3. The model's predictions are also supported by observations of high-energy astrophysical objects, such as active galactic nuclei, which exhibit a phenomenon of bipolar jets. Furthermore, the model's unique gravitational laws are shown to be consistent with other observed phenomena, such as the stability of stars and the stability of planetary systems.

The phenomenon of fast radio bursts is still not fully understood, but if these bursts originate from the Crab pulsar's magnetosphere, we can use this knowledge to set constraints on other potential sources of FRBs based on their observed radio flux. By comparing the maximum flux of an optical transient to its radio flux, we can determine a limit on the maximum optical flux of FRBs. This approach is applied to several events, such as the FRB 20200521A, where optical emission is constrained to a maximum of 10^(-4) the Crab's energy, and a nearby FRB 20220328, where it is constrained to a maximum of 10^(-5) the Crab's energy. This method is powerful for setting constraints on FRB optical emission, particularly for events that occur simultaneously with X-ray emission, like the neutron star merger AT2018cow. This approach is also applicable to the study of FRB optical emission in the context of the galaxy NGC 1275, where the maximum optical flux of FRBs is constrained to a maximum of 10^(-4) the Crab's energy. This constraint is particularly powerful for ruling out certain models of FRB optical emission, such as the neutron star merger model.
